title: The Migrating Pain
personal: Sarah Mitchell, 22, Female, 165 cm, 58 kg, final-year art student. Admitted to ward 4B this evening under case number MP-2291.
incident: It started as a dull ache circling her navel, the kind she blamed on a late lunch eaten too fast between critiques. She almost didn't mention it at all. But twelve hours later the pain had packed its bags and moved — settling low and sharp on her right side, just above the hip bone, as if it had finally found where it wanted to stay. Her appetite disappeared somewhere around dinner, and not long after, dinner disappeared too, once, into a hallway bin. Walking hurt. Bending hurt more. Coughing, she said, felt like being kicked from the inside by something that knew exactly where to aim. By the time her roommate called it in, she was curled on the bathroom floor, forehead damp, refusing point-blank to straighten her right leg. No blood in what she'd brought up, no diarrhea, nothing she could point to that made sense of it.
background: When the doctor sat down to take a fuller history, Sarah answered slowly, still wincing every few minutes. Her last period, she said, had been two weeks ago, right on schedule — she wasn't the type to lose track of that. She'd been with her boyfriend for over a year, and yes, they were sexually active, though she admitted with a small, embarrassed laugh that they didn't always remember protection. She'd never had anything like this before — no surgeries, no chronic conditions, nothing worth mentioning until tonight. Her mother, she added, had her gallbladder taken out years back, for whatever that was worth. She didn't smoke, had a glass of wine here and there, and admitted the timing was rotten — finals were this week. Oh, and her roommate had come down with some kind of stomach bug about ten days ago, though it had passed on its own after a couple of days.

exam.title: General
exam.body: The doctor began with a general examination, watching how Sarah held herself before even laying a hand on her. She lay curled on the trolley, knees drawn toward her chest, flinching at anything that came too close. Her temperature read 37.8°C, her pulse ticked along at 96 beats a minute, and her blood pressure sat at a steady 112 over 70. She looked unwell, certainly — but not gravely so. More like someone bracing for pain than someone in real danger.

exam.title: Abdominal
exam.body: Moving to the abdomen, the doctor pressed gently over the point just above her right hip bone, and Sarah's breath caught sharply. Letting go hurt even worse than pressing down had — the kind of rebound doctors take seriously. Asking her to lift her right leg against resistance brought the same wince back. There was no lump to feel anywhere, and — thankfully — no board-like rigidity across her belly, which would have meant something far more urgent than what this looked like.

exam.title: Pelvic, chaperoned
exam.body: With a chaperone present, the doctor carried out a pelvic examination too, checking whether the reproductive organs might be behind all this. There was no unusual discharge, no tenderness when the cervix was gently moved side to side, and nothing that felt like a mass or swelling on either side.

exam.title: Cardiovascular
exam.body: A quick listen to her heart turned up a steady, regular rhythm, no murmurs, and pulses that felt strong and even on both sides of her body.

exam.title: Respiratory
exam.body: Her lungs sounded clear on both sides too, with nothing to suggest her breathing discomfort had anything to do with her chest rather than the pain radiating up from below.

investigations.title: Laboratory
investigations.body: Blood was drawn and sent off within the hour, along with a urine sample to rule out a couple of other possibilities. This is what came back:

reports.title: Laboratory Report
lines: White cell count: 14,200/µL, neutrophil-predominant
Hemoglobin: within normal range
Platelets: within normal range
CRP: 42 mg/L (elevated)
Urine β-hCG: negative
Urinalysis: clean, no signs of infection

investigations.title: Imaging
investigations.body: An ultrasound followed shortly after, to get a clearer look at what was going on beneath the tenderness. The radiographer's findings:

reports.title: Imaging Report
lines: Right iliac fossa: non-compressible, blind-ending tubular structure, 9 mm diameter, surrounding fat stranding
Pelvis: no free fluid
Both ovaries: normal size and echotexture

treatment: The surgical team decided the safest course was to take her to theatre for a closer look. Working through three small incisions, they found what had been causing the trouble, dealt with it carefully, and left everything around it undisturbed and healthy. There was no rupture, no pus, nothing that had spread beyond where it started. By the next morning, her fever had settled on its own, her appetite was creeping back before breakfast even arrived, and she was already asking when she could go home rather than asking for more pain relief.
discharge: The pathology report landed on her chart the following afternoon, quietly confirming what the surgical team had suspected all along — an inflamed appendix, caught early, with clean margins and no sign of rupture or spread. Sarah went home on day two, three small dressings taped along her side, a stack of wound-care instructions in hand, and strict orders to stay off the gym for a couple of weeks.
dd1: Ruptured ovarian cyst or Ovarian torsion

title: The Missed Period That Wasn't
personal: Maya Torres, 27, Female, 160 cm, 55 kg, waitress. Brought in by ambulance, monitored closely on arrival.
incident: It had started as a sharp twinge low on her left side while she was clearing tables, the kind of pain she assumed was just a pulled muscle from lifting trays all shift. She pushed through the rest of her shift, and by the time she got home the ache had faded to something almost bearable. Two hours later it came back with a vengeance, and this time it brought the room spinning with it — she felt herself going lightheaded, broke into a cold sweat, and had to grip the kitchen counter to keep from going down. Lying on the sofa afterward, she noticed something odd: a strange ache in her shoulder, of all places, one that seemed worse the flatter she lay. She'd had some spotting over the past few days too, lighter and browner than her usual period, which she'd chalked up to stress.
background: Pressed gently for more detail, Maya admitted her last period had come seven weeks ago — later than her usual cycle, though she hadn't thought much of it at the time. She wasn't using any regular contraception; things with her new boyfriend had been "on and off, careful some of the time." She hadn't taken a pregnancy test. Two years ago she'd been treated for a chlamydia infection picked up from a previous partner, fully resolved at the time as far as she knew. No prior ectopic pregnancies, no surgeries, nothing else of note.

exam.title: General
exam.body: The doctor began with a general look-over before touching her at all. Maya was pale and clammy, restless on the trolley, her blood pressure reading a worryingly low 88 over 54 while her heart raced along at 128 beats a minute. Her hands felt cool despite the warm room, and there was a rawness of fear in how she kept asking if she was going to be okay.

exam.title: Abdominal
exam.body: Palpating her lower abdomen, the doctor found firm, guarded tenderness on the left side, worse than anywhere else, with a faint suggestion of rebound when the pressure was released. Asked to lie flatter for the exam, Maya complained again of that odd shoulder-tip ache — a small detail the doctor noted carefully, since pain referred to the shoulder can mean irritation reaching all the way up under the diaphragm.

exam.title: Pelvic, chaperoned
exam.body: With a chaperone in the room, a pelvic exam followed. Gently moving the cervix side to side brought a sharp intake of breath from Maya — a positive sign the doctor took seriously. A small amount of dark blood was visible, and deeper palpation on the left revealed an area of tender fullness that didn't feel like it belonged to the ovary alone.

exam.title: Cardiovascular
exam.body: Her pulse was rapid and thin under the doctor's fingers, though her heart sounds themselves were otherwise unremarkable — no murmurs, just a heart working hard to keep up.

investigations.title: Laboratory
investigations.body: A urine sample was sent first, along with blood for a more precise reading of the same hormone and a full blood count. The results came back within the hour:

reports.title: Laboratory Report
lines: Urine β-hCG: positive
Serum β-hCG: positive (confirms pregnancy)
Hemoglobin: 9.2 g/dL (low)
Group & crossmatch: sent, blood held in reserve

investigations.title: Imaging
investigations.body: An internal ultrasound scan followed shortly after, to work out exactly where the pregnancy was sitting:

reports.title: Imaging Report
lines: Uterus: empty
Pelvis: free fluid present, suggestive of bleeding
Left adnexa: complex, irregular mass, separate from the ovary

treatment: Within the hour, Maya was on her way to theatre. Working through small incisions, the surgical team located the source of the bleeding, brought it under control, and carefully removed the affected structure while leaving everything else untouched. She received a transfusion of blood to replace what she'd lost. Almost as soon as the bleeding was controlled, her blood pressure began climbing back toward normal, and the grey pallor slowly left her face.
discharge: Maya's recovery over the following two days was steady and uncomplicated. Before she left, the team spent time talking with her about what had happened, what it might mean for future pregnancies given the surgery to one of her tubes, and the importance of an early scan the next time she thinks she might be pregnant.
dd1: Ruptured ovarian cyst or Ovarian torsion

title: The Gallbladder Twinge That Didn't Quit
personal: Denise Cole, 45, Female, 168 cm, 88 kg, office manager. Admitted to the surgical ward this evening.
incident: Denise had felt this kind of pain before — a nagging ache under her right ribs that showed up now and then after a heavy meal, always fading within an hour or two if she just waited it out. Last night's version didn't play by the same rules. It started after dinner, the same dull throb she recognized, but instead of easing off it dug in and grew sharper over the following hours, until by morning it had become a constant, gripping pain that made her double over just walking to the bathroom. Chills came on through the night, alternating with a clammy warmth, and she brought up her breakfast once, unable to keep even water down afterward.
background: She'd had episodes like the milder version of this for a couple of years, always after fatty food — fried chicken, creamy pasta, that sort of thing — and had simply learned to avoid those meals rather than get it looked at. She hadn't noticed her urine looking darker or her stools looking pale, hadn't noticed any yellowing of her eyes. No history of alcohol excess. She was a mother of three, generally busy enough that a doctor's visit for "just some twinges" had never made it to the top of her list.

exam.title: General
exam.body: The doctor's first impression was of someone clearly unwell — flushed, sweating lightly, with a temperature reading of 38.6°C. Her pulse sat at 104, her blood pressure a little elevated at 130 over 84, and there was no yellow tinge visible in her eyes when the doctor checked.

exam.title: Abdominal
exam.body: Asking Denise to take a deep breath in while pressing gently under her right ribcage, the doctor watched her breath catch abruptly halfway through, unable to continue — a sign doctors specifically look for when they suspect trouble with the gallbladder. There was no spreading rigidity across the rest of her abdomen, and no rebound tenderness elsewhere.

exam.title: Respiratory
exam.body: Listening to both lungs, the doctor heard clear air entry throughout, no crackles, no signs that anything in her chest might be responsible for pain reaching around to her right side.

exam.title: Cardiovascular
exam.body: Heart sounds were normal, rhythm regular, nothing to suggest a cardiac cause for her discomfort.

investigations.title: Laboratory
investigations.body: Blood was drawn to check her inflammatory markers, liver function, and pancreatic enzymes together. The panel came back as follows:

reports.title: Laboratory Report
lines: White cell count: raised
CRP: elevated
ALT/AST: mildly raised
Bilirubin and ALP: within normal limits
Amylase/lipase: normal

investigations.title: Imaging
investigations.body: An ultrasound of her abdomen was arranged to look directly at the gallbladder and bile ducts:

reports.title: Imaging Report
lines: Gallbladder wall: thickened
Pericholecystic fluid: small amount present
Gallstones: multiple, visible within the gallbladder
Sonographic Murphy's sign: positive
Common bile duct: normal caliber throughout

treatment: Denise was started on fluids through a drip and a course of antibiotics while the team monitored how she responded. Her pain settled steadily over the following day, and once the surgical team judged the inflammation had calmed enough to operate safely, she was taken for a keyhole procedure during the same admission. She was up and moving, tolerating food again, well before the day was out.
discharge: Denise went home two days later, her small keyhole scars healing cleanly, with advice to ease back into a normal diet gradually. The surgical team reassured her that, gallbladder removed, the twinges she'd been living with for two years wouldn't be coming back.

title: The Long Flight Home
personal: Priya Anand, 34, Female, 165 cm, 70 kg, flight attendant. Admitted to the respiratory ward.
incident: She'd landed from a ten-hour flight feeling fine, if a little stiff from all the standing. It was only once she got home that the trouble started — a breathlessness that crept up on her out of nowhere, paired with a sharp stab of pain on the right side of her chest that flared every time she took a deep breath. Thinking back, she realized her right calf had been aching for a couple of days before the flight too, something she'd put down to being on her feet all shift, now looking noticeably more swollen than the left when she finally looked closely.
background: Priya had been on the combined contraceptive pill for years without any issues, and smoked around ten cigarettes a day, a habit she'd never quite managed to shake despite her job. She had no previous history of blood clots, no recent surgery, and nothing else unusual — just the long flight, the pill, and the cigarettes, three things that don't sit well together.

exam.title: General
exam.body: She looked anxious and breathless even sitting still, working visibly to draw each breath. Her oxygen level read 91% on room air, her heart rate sat at 118, blood pressure 108 over 70, and there was a faint bluish tinge to her lips that hadn't been there before.

exam.title: Respiratory
exam.body: Listening carefully to her chest, the doctor found both sides moving and filling equally, clear air entry with no crackles or wheeze, and no area of dullness that might suggest fluid or a collapsed lung hiding underneath.

exam.title: Cardiovascular
exam.body: Her heart raced but kept a steady rhythm, no murmurs audible — though the doctor did note something subtle: the second heart sound had an unusually loud component on the left side of the chest, a small clue that the right side of her heart might be working harder than it should.

exam.title: Lower limb
exam.body: Comparing both calves side by side, the right was visibly larger than the left, warm to the touch, and tender along the length of the deep veins running behind the knee and down the calf.

investigations.title: Laboratory
investigations.body: Blood was sent for a clot marker, a blood gas sample, and a heart-strain marker, alongside a routine count:

reports.title: Laboratory Report
lines: D-dimer: markedly elevated
Arterial blood gas: low oxygen, widened alveolar-arterial gradient
Troponin: mildly elevated
White cell count: normal

investigations.title: Imaging
investigations.body: A CT scan of the chest and an ultrasound of her legs were both arranged the same afternoon:

reports.title: Imaging Report
lines: Right pulmonary arterial tree: multiple filling defects consistent with clot
Right femoral vein: thrombus confirmed on Doppler ultrasound

treatment: Priya was started straight away on medication and given oxygen through a mask while her breathing was monitored closely for the first day. Over the following 48 hours, her oxygen levels crept back up on their own, the stabbing chest pain eased with each breath, and the color returned to her lips.
discharge: She was discharged on ongoing blood thinners, with clear advice to come off the contraceptive pill and discuss safer alternatives, and firm encouragement to use her next long flight as the moment to finally quit smoking for good.

title: Too Quiet for a Baby
personal: Noah Ferreira, 8 months, Male, 70 cm, 8.5 kg, infant. Admitted to the pediatric intensive care unit.
incident: For two days Noah had been fussier than usual, feeding poorly, nothing his mother could quite put her finger on. Today a fever set in properly, and by the afternoon something had clearly shifted — he'd gone unusually floppy in her arms, hard to console no matter what she tried, crying out sharply whenever she lifted him under the arms as she always did, and arching his back away from her in a way she'd never seen before.
background: Noah was born full term with no complications and had met every milestone so far. His vaccinations were up to date for his age, though the doctor noted that the particular boosters that guard most strongly against this kind of illness aren't fully completed until a little later in infancy. No sick contacts at home, no daycare yet, and no rash that his mother had spotted before they left the house.

exam.title: General
exam.body: The doctor's first look told a worrying story — a high fever of 39.4°C, a baby too lethargic to make proper eye contact, a weak and reedy cry, and a capillary refill that took a touch longer than it should when the doctor pressed gently on his skin.

exam.title: Neurological
exam.body: Checking his soft spot, the doctor found it firm and slightly bulging rather than the normal gentle dip — a significant finding in an infant this age. He was markedly irritable to being handled, and when lifted, his back arched away rigidly instead of curling naturally, a posture doctors watch for carefully in babies who can't yet tell you their neck hurts.

exam.title: Skin
exam.body: Undressed fully under the ward lights, his skin was checked from head to toe for the kind of rash that can signal a particularly dangerous strain of this illness. None was found anywhere.

exam.title: Respiratory/Cardiovascular
exam.body: His chest was clear, his heart sounds normal, with a heart rate a little fast but entirely explained by the fever alone.

investigations.title: Laboratory
investigations.body: Blood was drawn for routine markers, and once it was judged safe, a lumbar puncture was performed to sample the fluid around his brain and spinal cord:

reports.title: Laboratory Report
lines: White cell count: markedly elevated
CRP: markedly elevated
CSF appearance: cloudy
CSF white cells: very high, neutrophil-dominant
CSF protein: raised
CSF glucose: low relative to blood glucose

investigations.title: Imaging
investigations.body: Before the lumbar puncture, an ultrasound scan through his still-open soft spot was carried out, to make sure it was safe to proceed:

reports.title: Imaging Report
lines: Intracranial pressure: no signs of dangerous elevation
Ventricles: normal size
No mass identified

treatment: Noah was started immediately on strong intravenous antibiotics, along with fluids to support him and constant monitoring in intensive care. Over the following two days, his fever gradually broke, his eyes began following his mother's face again, and he started taking his bottle a little at a time.
discharge: He completed the rest of his antibiotic course in hospital, and before going home a hearing test was arranged, since this kind of infection can occasionally leave that particular after-effect. His parents left with a plan to catch up on the remaining scheduled vaccinations and a follow-up appointment to check on his development.

title: Doubled Over at Practice
personal: Chloe Bennett, 15, Female, 158 cm, 50 kg, high school student and competitive gymnast. Admitted to the gynecology ward.
incident: It hit her mid-cartwheel, of all moments — a sudden, tearing pain low on her left side that made her crumple to the mat instead of landing on her feet. Her coach thought at first she'd pulled something, but the pain didn't behave like a muscle strain; it came in intense, rolling waves, each one making her curl tighter into herself, and within twenty minutes she'd been sick twice from how much it hurt. She kept telling her mother, on the drive to hospital, that this was nothing like even her worst period cramps.
background: Her periods had started at twelve and had been fairly regular since. Asked gently and privately, she confirmed she wasn't sexually active. No fever, no burning when she went to the bathroom, no history of ovarian cysts that anyone had mentioned to her before. Otherwise a healthy, fit teenager who trained most days of the week.

exam.title: General
exam.body: Chloe couldn't hold still on the trolley, rocking and shifting in search of any position that hurt less. Her temperature read a normal 37.1°C, ruling out a raging infection at this stage, though her heart rate had climbed to 108 — understandable for someone in this much pain.

exam.title: Abdominal
exam.body: Palpating carefully, the doctor found clear tenderness low on the left side, with a subtle sense of fullness felt on deeper pressure that wasn't present on the right. There was no rigidity and no rebound tenderness to suggest anything had ruptured through the abdominal wall's lining.

exam.title: Pelvic
exam.body: Given her age, the assessment here was kept brief and appropriate, performed with her mother present — no discharge was seen, and the exam was limited to what was necessary given how much distress she was already in.

investigations.title: Laboratory
investigations.body: A urine sample and a set of blood markers were sent to help narrow things down:

reports.title: Laboratory Report
lines: Urine pregnancy test: negative
Urinalysis: clean
White cell count: mildly raised
CRP: mildly raised

investigations.title: Imaging
investigations.body: An ultrasound with a blood-flow study followed, aimed squarely at the ovary itself:

reports.title: Imaging Report
lines: Left ovary: significantly enlarged compared with the right, with a cyst visible inside
Doppler blood flow to the left ovary: absent to minimal

treatment: Chloe was taken urgently to theatre. Working through small keyhole incisions, the surgical team found what they'd suspected, carefully released it, and waited to watch the color return before deciding it was healthy enough to leave in place rather than remove. She woke from the anesthetic already reporting the pain as far more manageable than before she went in.
discharge: She went home the following day, the affected ovary preserved and expected to work normally going forward. Her family was advised on the small chance this could happen again in the future, and told to come straight back in if that same tearing pain ever returned.

title: Woken by the Pain
personal: Tyler James, 14, Male, 160 cm, 48 kg, secondary school student. Admitted to the urology ward via the emergency department.
incident: Tyler woke around midnight with a pain unlike anything he'd felt before, sharp and severe, low in his groin, bad enough that he was too embarrassed to say anything at first and just lay there hoping it would pass. It didn't. Nausea followed, then a single episode of vomiting, and by the time he finally worked up the courage to wake his father, three hours had already gone by.
background: No injury, no recent sport where he might have been struck, no burning or urgency with urination. On further questioning, though, he mentioned — almost as an afterthought — that he'd had a couple of brief, similar aches in the past that settled on their own within a few minutes and hadn't seemed worth mentioning at the time. He wasn't sexually active, and there had been no fever noticed at home.

exam.title: General
exam.body: Tyler was pale and clearly trying to hold himself together, nauseated, with a normal temperature of 36.9°C — a detail that made an infectious cause somewhat less likely — and a heart rate of 100, understandably raised given the pain he was in.

exam.title: Genital
exam.body: Examining the area gently, the doctor found the right side sitting higher than the left and lying at an unusual horizontal angle, visibly swollen and so tender that even the lightest touch made Tyler flinch away. Lifting the affected side gently, rather than easing the discomfort as it would with an infection, made no difference at all. A reflex normally present on stroking the inner thigh could not be found on that side.

exam.title: Abdominal
exam.body: His abdomen was soft and non-tender throughout, with no swelling in the groin to suggest a hernia pushing through.

investigations.title: Imaging
investigations.body: Because every minute matters with this kind of pain, the surgical team didn't wait for imaging to confirm what the examination already strongly suggested, and arranged to go straight to theatre. A scan requested in parallel, done just before he went in, showed the following:

reports.title: Imaging Report
lines: Right testicle: absent to minimal blood flow on Doppler ultrasound

investigations.title: Laboratory
investigations.body: A urine sample and basic bloods were sent alongside:

reports.title: Laboratory Report
lines: Urinalysis: clean
White cell count: normal
CRP: normal

treatment: Tyler was taken to theatre without further delay. The surgical team found what had happened, carefully corrected it, and waited to see healthy color return before deciding it was worth preserving. To prevent anything like this from happening again, both sides were secured in place before he was closed up. He woke with the pain already dramatically eased.
discharge: He went home the next day with simple pain relief and instructions to avoid sport for a few weeks while things healed. Both sides had been preserved, and his family was reassured that the stitching in place now meant this particular emergency shouldn't recur.

title: Leaning Forward to Breathe
personal: Sofia Marin, 3, Female, 96 cm, 15 kg, nursery attendee. Admitted to the pediatric high dependency unit.
incident: Sofia had seemed perfectly well at nursery pickup. Within a few hours at home, a sore throat turned into a raging fever, and by evening she had stopped swallowing altogether, drooling steadily onto her bib because it hurt too much even to swallow her own saliva. Her parents found her sitting bolt upright on the sofa, leaning forward with her chin jutted out, making a strange soft, muffled sound with every breath that neither of them had heard from her before.
background: A missed vaccination appointment as a baby, never rescheduled amid the usual chaos of early parenthood, meant Sofia hadn't received one of the vaccines that most strongly protects against this particular illness. She'd been entirely well before today, no known allergies, no choking episode that anyone had witnessed, and — notably — no cough at all, which struck the triage nurse as unusual for a child this unwell.

exam.title: General
exam.body: The doctor deliberately kept their distance at first, watching rather than touching. Sofia sat rigidly upright, leaning forward, drooling steadily, a soft rasping noise audible with every breath even without a stethoscope, her temperature reading a striking 39.6°C. She looked frightened, and frighteningly unwell.

exam.title: Respiratory
exam.body: Watching her breathe rather than disturbing her position, the doctor noted mild tugging at the base of her neck with each breath in, no barking cough at any point, and no wheeze — all details that steered the picture away from the more common causes of noisy breathing in small children.

exam.title: ENT
exam.body: A direct look inside her mouth and throat was deliberately avoided. In a child this unwell with this kind of breathing, forcing an examination of the throat can be enough to trigger the airway to close completely, so the team held off until an anesthetist was present and ready to help if needed.

investigations.title: Airway
investigations.body: With an anesthetist standing by in a controlled theatre setting, a careful look at the back of her throat was finally taken, and a breathing tube placed at the same time to keep her airway safely open:

reports.title: Airway Report
lines: Supraglottic structure: swollen, deep red in appearance, consistent with the suspected cause of obstruction
Airway secured with a tube without complication

investigations.title: Laboratory
investigations.body: Once she was safely stabilized, blood cultures and a swab from her airway were sent off:

reports.title: Laboratory Report
lines: Blood cultures: later grew a bacterium well known for causing exactly this kind of presentation
Airway swab: same organism isolated

treatment: Sofia was kept sedated with the breathing tube in place for a few days in intensive care while strong antibiotics were given through a drip, and the swelling in her throat was checked periodically. Once the team judged it had settled enough, the tube was carefully removed with everyone standing ready in case it was needed again. She came through it breathing comfortably entirely on her own.
discharge: She finished her antibiotic course before leaving hospital, and before discharge her family made sure she was caught up on the vaccination she'd missed as a baby, with the team gently explaining just how much that one appointment could have changed.

title: Not Himself Today
personal: Harold Whitmore, 82, Male, 170 cm, 68 kg, retired postman, lives alone. Admitted to the acute medical unit.
incident: For three days Harold's cough had been getting worse, bringing up sputum that had turned an unusual rust color, along with fevers that came and went with bouts of shivering he couldn't seem to shake off. It was his daughter, visiting today as she always did on Thursdays, who found him confused and unsteady on his feet, unable to say clearly what day it was — utterly unlike the sharp, independent man she was used to.
background: Harold lived alone and managed well by himself under normal circumstances. He had mild high blood pressure controlled with tablets, no known lung disease, and hadn't smoked in twenty years, though he'd smoked heavily for decades before quitting. He'd had his flu vaccine this year but had never gotten around to the other vaccine his doctor had mentioned for his chest, and he hadn't been in hospital for anything in a long while.

exam.title: General
exam.body: Harold was confused when the doctor spoke to him, unable to say the correct day or where he was. His temperature read 38.9°C, his heart racing at 116, his blood pressure sitting low at 96 over 58, and his breathing quick at 28 breaths a minute. He looked unwell and dried out, his lips slightly cracked.

exam.title: Respiratory
exam.body: Listening to his back, the doctor found reduced air movement and crackling sounds low down on the right side, a dull note when tapping over the same area, and the sound of his voice carrying unusually clearly through the stethoscope there too — all signs that something was filling that part of the lung rather than air.

exam.title: Cardiovascular
exam.body: His heart sounds were unremarkable, no murmurs, and there was no swelling in his ankles to suggest fluid backing up from a struggling heart.

exam.title: Abdominal/Urinary
exam.body: His abdomen was soft throughout with no tenderness, and no discomfort when the doctor pressed over either side of his lower back where the kidneys sit.

investigations.title: Laboratory
investigations.body: Blood and urine were both sent off to help settle which source was to blame:

reports.title: Laboratory Report
lines: White cell count: sharply raised
CRP: sharply raised
Urea and creatinine: raised above his usual baseline
Lactate: mildly elevated
Urinalysis and urine culture: unremarkable
Blood cultures: sent

investigations.title: Imaging
investigations.body: A chest X-ray was taken to confirm where the trouble was sitting:

reports.title: Imaging Report
lines: Lower right lung: patch of consolidation
No evidence of fluid overload elsewhere in the lungs

treatment: Harold was started straight away on fluids through a drip alongside antibiotics, with his blood pressure and confusion checked at regular intervals through the night. By the second day, his fevers had settled, his blood pressure had climbed back to a healthy range, and his daughter arrived to find him asking after his prize tomato plants instead of asking where he was.
discharge: He completed his course of antibiotics and was discharged home with a community nurse arranged to check in on him over the following weeks. Before he left, he was finally given the vaccine he'd never quite gotten around to, with a gentle reminder of why it mattered.

title: The Baby Had Gone Quiet
personal: Amara Johnson, 32, Female, 165 cm, 78 kg (pregnant), graphic designer, 34 weeks into her second pregnancy. Admitted to the maternity assessment unit.
incident: The pain arrived without warning — constant, gripping, and entirely unlike the tightenings she remembered from her first pregnancy, which used to come and go in waves. Alongside it came a small trickle of dark blood, enough to worry her but not enough, she thought, to be anything serious. What frightened her most was the stillness: her baby, usually a whirlwind of movement by this time in the evening, hadn't stirred once since the pain began.
background: This pregnancy had gone smoothly so far, with normal blood pressure readings at every appointment until a slightly raised one two weeks ago that nobody had followed up on with any urgency. She didn't smoke and hadn't used any recreational drugs, hadn't fallen or been in any accident, and her first pregnancy had ended in a straightforward vaginal delivery with no complications.

exam.title: General
exam.body: Amara looked frightened and pale, clutching her abdomen. Her blood pressure read 148 over 96 — notably higher than any reading she'd had before — and her heart rate had climbed to 104.

exam.title: Abdominal/Obstetric
exam.body: Feeling her uterus, the doctor found it unusually firm throughout, tender everywhere it was touched, and — unlike a normal contraction — it never relaxed between what should have been separate tightenings. This constant rigidity, sometimes described as feeling almost woody to the touch, made it difficult even to work out how the baby was lying inside.

exam.title: Fetal assessment
exam.body: A monitor was strapped to her abdomen to trace the baby's heartbeat continuously. The pattern that emerged showed less variation than it should, with occasional dips that suggested the baby wasn't getting quite the oxygen supply it needed.

exam.title: Vaginal
exam.body: A small amount of dark blood was confirmed at the vaginal opening. An internal examination of the cervix was deliberately held off given the bleeding, pending a clearer picture of what was happening higher up.

investigations.title: Laboratory
investigations.body: Blood was sent urgently to check her clotting, blood count, and organ function given how high her blood pressure had climbed:

reports.title: Laboratory Report
lines: Hemoglobin: mildly reduced from her booking level
Clotting screen: sent urgently, results pending given the risk this condition carries
Group & crossmatch: sent
Kidney and liver function: checked given the raised blood pressure

investigations.title: Imaging
investigations.body: An ultrasound was attempted, with its limitations for this particular diagnosis explained to Amara beforehand:

reports.title: Imaging Report
lines: Placenta: possible area of separation from the uterine wall noted
Scan noted as an imperfect tool for confirming this diagnosis; clinical picture weighted more heavily

treatment: Given the pattern on the baby's heart trace and the overall clinical picture, the team moved quickly to deliver by emergency cesarean section rather than wait any longer. The baby was delivered promptly, needed a little help getting started with breathing, and was soon settled comfortably in the neonatal unit. Once the womb was empty, the bleeding that had worried everyone came under control.
discharge: Both mother and baby did well over the following days, the baby kept in for a short spell of monitoring given the early arrival. Before Amara went home, the team talked through what had happened and the closer blood pressure monitoring she'd need in any future pregnancy.

title: Legs That Wouldn't Cooperate
personal: Kevin O'Brien, 45, Male, 176 cm, 82 kg, accountant. Admitted to the neurology ward.
incident: It began four days ago as an odd tingling in both feet, the sort of pins-and-needles feeling he assumed would pass on its own. Instead, it crept steadily upward, day by day, into his shins and then his thighs, until this morning he found himself gripping the stair rail with both hands, his legs suddenly feeling heavy and unreliable in a way that frightened him enough to head straight to the hospital rather than wait it out any longer.
background: About two and a half weeks earlier, Kevin had come down with a stomach bug he'd blamed on a work lunch — a few days of diarrhea that settled on its own without treatment. Otherwise, he had no significant medical history, no recent vaccinations, no back pain, and — so far, at least — no trouble with his bladder or bowels. Nobody in his family had ever had anything like this.

exam.title: General
exam.body: Kevin was alert and clearly anxious about his legs, though his speech and swallowing were entirely normal, his vital signs stable, and his breathing comfortable while sitting at rest.

exam.title: Neurological — motor
exam.body: Testing his strength throughout, the doctor found both legs weaker than they should be, more so at the ankles than up near the hips, and on closer testing found a milder version of the same weakness had begun creeping into his hands too. Tapping for reflexes at both the knees and ankles produced nothing at all on either side.

exam.title: Neurological — sensory
exam.body: Testing light touch and pinprick sensation, the doctor found it reduced over both feet and lower legs in a pattern that looked almost like he was wearing an invisible pair of socks, symmetrical on both sides.

exam.title: Respiratory
exam.body: His chest sounded clear, but given the specific risk this condition carries for the muscles involved in breathing, the doctor measured exactly how forcefully he could blow out in one breath, finding it slightly below what would be expected for someone his size.

investigations.title: Laboratory
investigations.body: A sample of fluid was drawn from around his spinal cord, alongside routine blood tests:

reports.title: Laboratory Report
lines: CSF protein: raised
CSF white cell count: normal
Blood electrolytes: normal
Other routine bloods: unremarkable

investigations.title: Nerve Conduction
investigations.body: Studies measuring how quickly signals traveled along his nerves were carried out on both his arms and legs:

reports.title: Nerve Conduction Report
lines: Conduction velocities: slowed throughout
Pattern consistent with the insulating coating around the nerves being affected, rather than the nerves themselves being structurally damaged

treatment: Kevin was started promptly on a course of infusion treatment aimed at calming down the immune response responsible for his weakness, with his breathing strength checked several times a day in case it began to slip further. Physiotherapy was brought in early to keep his joints moving and his muscles as ready as possible for when his strength began to return, which it slowly did over the following two weeks.
discharge: Once his breathing was confirmed stable and he could stand with support, Kevin was transferred to a rehabilitation unit to continue his recovery, with physiotherapy continuing as an outpatient. Most people who go through what he did make substantial recoveries over the following months, and his team were quietly optimistic about his outlook.

title: Wrong Side of the Belly
personal: Walter Grimes, 67, Male, 174 cm, 84 kg, retired librarian. Admitted to the surgical assessment unit.
incident: It started two days ago as a mild ache low on his left side, the kind he'd assumed was just something he'd eaten disagreeing with him. Instead of settling, it had crept steadily worse, and by this morning it had become a constant, gnawing pain that made him wince every time he shifted position on the sofa. He'd noticed his bowel habits had been irregular for a while now, sometimes constipated for days at a stretch, and last night he'd had a fever that left the sheets damp by morning.
background: Walter admitted, a little sheepishly, that he'd known for a couple of years he had "pouches" somewhere in his large bowel — mentioned once at a routine check-up and then never followed up on. His diet, he conceded, had never been particularly high in fibre. No prior surgeries, no blood in his stool that he'd noticed, no weight loss. He took a tablet for his blood pressure and nothing else regularly.

exam.title: General
exam.body: Walter looked uncomfortable but not acutely unwell, holding himself carefully as he walked into the room. His temperature read 38.2°C, his pulse 98, blood pressure 134 over 82.

exam.title: Abdominal
exam.body: Pressing over his lower left abdomen, the doctor found firm, localized tenderness with mild guarding, and — unusually for the other side of the abdomen where this kind of tenderness more commonly shows up — no findings at all on the right. There was no rigid, board-like abdomen, and no mass felt, though the area was clearly unhappy about being touched.

exam.title: Rectal
exam.body: A gentle rectal examination revealed no blood, no obvious mass, and confirmed tenderness could be felt higher up on the left when pressed toward that side.

investigations.title: Laboratory
investigations.body: Blood was drawn to look for signs of active infection or inflammation:

reports.title: Laboratory Report
lines: White cell count: raised
CRP: markedly elevated
Hemoglobin: normal, no evidence of chronic bleeding
Renal function: normal

investigations.title: Imaging
investigations.body: A CT scan of his abdomen and pelvis was arranged to get a clear look at the bowel itself:

reports.title: Imaging Report
lines: Sigmoid colon: wall thickening with surrounding fat stranding, several small outpouchings visible along its length
No abscess
No free air, no evidence of perforation
No mass identified

treatment: Walter was admitted for a course of intravenous antibiotics and bowel rest, with his pain, temperature, and blood markers checked daily. Over the following three days his fever settled, his appetite slowly returned, and the tenderness in his abdomen eased enough for him to walk comfortably around the ward.
discharge: He was discharged on oral antibiotics to finish the course at home, with a plan for a colonoscopy in six weeks once the inflammation had fully settled, both to confirm the diagnosis directly and to make sure nothing else was hiding underneath it. He was also referred to a dietitian to talk through ways of increasing the fibre in his diet.

title: Crushing, Straight Through
personal: Frank Delaney, 58, Male, 177 cm, 95 kg, delivery driver. Brought in by ambulance to the coronary care unit.
incident: He'd been loading his van when it hit — a heavy, crushing pressure across the center of his chest, like someone standing on it, spreading up into his jaw and down his left arm. He'd tried to shrug it off at first, thinking it was just indigestion from the sausage roll he'd grabbed for breakfast, but it didn't ease, and within minutes he was sweating heavily and felt sick to his stomach. A colleague found him leaning against the van, grey-faced, and called an ambulance without waiting for him to argue.
background: Frank had high blood pressure and high cholesterol, both "on and off" treated depending on whether he remembered to collect his prescriptions. He smoked around fifteen cigarettes a day and had done for thirty years. His father had a heart attack in his sixties. He'd had occasional chest tightness climbing stairs over the past couple of months that he'd put down to being unfit and never mentioned to anyone.

exam.title: General
exam.body: Frank was pale, sweating profusely, clutching his chest with a fist pressed to his sternum. His blood pressure read 98 over 62, his pulse 104 and slightly irregular, and he looked visibly frightened.

exam.title: Cardiovascular
exam.body: Heart sounds were difficult to assess clearly given how distressed he was, but no obvious murmur was heard, and there was no difference in blood pressure between his two arms — a detail the doctor checked specifically, since an unequal reading can point toward a tear in the main artery leaving the heart rather than a blocked one.

exam.title: Respiratory
exam.body: His chest was clear, with mild bibasal crackles at the very bottom of both lungs, suggesting his heart wasn't pumping quite as efficiently as it should at that moment.

investigations.title: Laboratory
investigations.body: Blood was sent immediately for a heart-muscle marker, alongside routine tests:

reports.title: Laboratory Report
lines: Troponin: markedly elevated
Full blood count: normal
Kidney function: normal

investigations.title: ECG
investigations.body: A tracing of his heart's electrical activity was taken within minutes of arrival:

reports.title: ECG Report
lines: ST-segment elevation across the inferior leads
Reciprocal ST depression in the anterior leads

treatment: Frank was rushed straight to an emergency procedure carried out through an artery in his wrist. His chest pain eased almost as soon as it was done, and by the next morning he was sitting up in bed, color back in his face, asking when he could have a proper breakfast.
discharge: He was discharged a few days later on a combination of heart medications, with a firm and detailed conversation about quitting smoking, controlling his blood pressure and cholesterol properly this time, and a referral to a cardiac rehabilitation program to help him get back on his feet safely.

title: The Wound That Wouldn't Heal
personal: Bernard Osei, 67, Male, 172 cm, 90 kg, retired bus driver. Admitted to the diabetic foot clinic ward.
incident: It had started as a small blister on the sole of his right foot after a long walk in new shoes, something he barely noticed at the time because, as he put it, "I never really feel much down there anyway." Weeks later, what should have healed had instead opened into a wound that wouldn't close, now weeping and increasingly foul-smelling, with the skin around it turning an angry red that had crept further up his foot over the past several days.
background: Bernard had lived with diabetes for close to twenty years, and admitted his blood sugar control had been "hit and miss" for a long stretch of that time. He'd noticed his feet had felt increasingly numb over the years, something he'd mentioned to his doctor in passing but never had properly assessed. No fever that he'd noticed at home, though he'd been feeling more tired than usual lately.

exam.title: General
exam.body: Bernard looked otherwise reasonably well, though a little fatigued, with a temperature of 37.6°C, pulse 88, and blood pressure within normal range.

exam.title: Foot examination
exam.body: On the sole of his right foot, the doctor found an ulcer roughly two centimeters across, with a probe passed gently into the wound reaching down to what felt like bone — a finding doctors take very seriously in exactly this situation. The surrounding skin was red, warm, and mildly swollen, though pulses could still be felt at the ankle, and sensation to light touch was markedly reduced across the whole foot.

exam.title: Vascular
exam.body: Checking blood flow further, pulses were present though a little weaker than ideal, and his toes remained warm and pink, arguing against a primarily blood-flow-related cause for the wound not healing.

investigations.title: Laboratory
investigations.body: Blood was sent to check his overall sugar control and look for markers of deep infection:

reports.title: Laboratory Report
lines: White cell count: mildly raised
CRP: elevated
HbA1c: significantly above target, reflecting poor long-term sugar control
Blood glucose on admission: elevated

investigations.title: Imaging
investigations.body: An X-ray of the foot was taken, followed by an MRI scan to look more closely at the bone underneath the wound:

reports.title: Imaging Report
lines: X-ray: subtle changes at the underlying bone
MRI: signal changes within the bone consistent with infection extending down from the wound above it

treatment: Bernard was started on a prolonged course of targeted antibiotics, with the wound cleaned and dressed regularly by the specialist foot team, and his blood sugar brought under much tighter control during the admission. Over the following weeks, the wound slowly began to shrink and the redness around it faded.
discharge: He completed a long course of antibiotics as an outpatient, with regular foot clinic follow-up arranged and a referral to a diabetes specialist team to help him manage his sugar levels going forward, along with education on daily foot checks to catch anything like this much earlier next time.

title: Sudden Back Pain, Then Nothing Steady
personal: Eugene Mackay, 74, Male, 175 cm, 80 kg, retired carpenter. Brought in by ambulance to the vascular surgery ward.
incident: He'd been standing at his workbench when a sudden, tearing pain ripped through his lower back and abdomen, dropping him to his knees. His wife found him moments later, pale and clammy, unable to stand back up, saying the pain felt like nothing he'd experienced before — worse, he said, than the time he broke his leg. By the time the ambulance arrived, he was starting to feel lightheaded.
background: Eugene had known for a few years about a "bulge" in one of his main blood vessels, mentioned at a routine scan and monitored periodically, though he admitted he'd missed his last two follow-up appointments. He'd smoked heavily for most of his adult life before quitting a decade ago, and had longstanding high blood pressure that he took medication for, though not always consistently.

exam.title: General
exam.body: Eugene was pale, sweating, and visibly frightened, with a blood pressure that had dropped to 84 over 50 and a heart rate racing at 122.

exam.title: Abdominal
exam.body: Gently pressing on his abdomen, the doctor could feel a pulsating mass just above his navel, tender to touch — a finding that immediately narrowed the list of possibilities down to something very specific and very urgent.

exam.title: Vascular
exam.body: Pulses in both legs were present but notably weaker than they should be, and his feet felt cooler to the touch than the rest of his body.

investigations.title: Laboratory
investigations.body: Given how time-critical the situation looked, only the most essential bloods were drawn while preparations for theatre began in parallel:

reports.title: Laboratory Report
lines: Hemoglobin: dropping on repeat testing
Group & crossmatch: urgent, large volume requested
Kidney function: mildly impaired

investigations.title: Imaging
investigations.body: A bedside ultrasound was performed within minutes, given how unstable he was:

reports.title: Imaging Report
lines: Abdominal aorta: significantly dilated, measuring well beyond the normal range
Free fluid: present around the aorta, suggestive of leakage

treatment: Eugene was rushed to theatre without delay, where the vascular surgical team worked to control the bleeding and repair what they found. He required significant blood transfusion during the operation and spent the following days in intensive care while his body recovered from the strain.
discharge: His recovery was slow but steady over the following two weeks, moving from intensive care to a general ward as his strength returned. Before discharge, his family was given a clear explanation of what had happened and firm advice about never missing a follow-up scan again.

title: Couldn't Go, Wouldn't Stop Trying
personal: Arthur Pemberton, 70, Male, 173 cm, 79 kg, retired schoolteacher. Admitted to the urology assessment unit.
incident: For the past several months, Arthur had noticed his usual trips to the bathroom had become more frequent, especially at night, along with a weaker stream and a nagging sense he'd never quite finished. Tonight, though, something different happened — despite feeling desperate to go, nothing would come out at all, and the pressure and pain in his lower abdomen had steadily built to the point where he was pacing the hallway, unable to sit still.
background: Arthur had mentioned the slow, gradual changes to his waterworks to his doctor a while back but hadn't followed up on the suggestion to get it looked at properly. No fever, no blood in his urine that he'd noticed, no back pain. He wasn't on any new medications recently and had no history of kidney stones or prior urinary problems before the last several months.

exam.title: General
exam.body: Arthur was clearly uncomfortable, shifting his weight from foot to foot, unable to find a position that eased the pressure. His temperature was normal, blood pressure and pulse only mildly raised, consistent with pain and anxiety rather than infection.

exam.title: Abdominal
exam.body: Just above his pubic bone, the doctor could feel and gently percuss a firm, rounded swelling — an unmistakably full bladder — with Arthur wincing the moment it was touched.

exam.title: Rectal
exam.body: A gentle rectal examination revealed a smoothly and evenly enlarged prostate, without any hard, irregular areas that might raise concern for something more sinister.

investigations.title: Laboratory
investigations.body: A urine sample was taken as soon as it was possible to obtain one, along with routine blood tests:

reports.title: Laboratory Report
lines: Urinalysis: clean, no signs of infection
Kidney function: mildly affected, likely from the back-pressure of a full bladder
Prostate-specific antigen: mildly raised, in keeping with an enlarged but non-cancerous gland

investigations.title: Imaging
investigations.body: An ultrasound of his bladder and kidneys was arranged once some of the pressure had been relieved:

reports.title: Imaging Report
lines: Bladder: markedly distended before drainage
Kidneys: mild swelling on both sides, consistent with back-pressure, no stones seen
Prostate: enlarged, smooth in contour

treatment: A thin tube was passed, bringing him near-instant relief. He was started on medication to treat the underlying cause over time, with the tube left in place temporarily while the medication took effect.
discharge: After a trial without the drainage tube proved successful a few days later, Arthur went home passing urine normally again, with ongoing medication and a referral to a urologist to discuss longer-term options for his enlarged prostate.
dd1: Acute urinary retention due to BPH
final: Acute urinary retention due to BPH

title: Five Days of Fever
personal: Mia Alvarez, 2, Female, 88 cm, 13 kg, toddler. Admitted to the pediatric ward.
incident: Mia had been running a high fever for five days straight now, nothing bringing it down for long despite regular medicine at home. Over the past two days her parents had noticed her eyes had turned strikingly red without any discharge, her lips had become cracked and unusually red, and today a blotchy rash had spread across her trunk. She'd also become increasingly irritable, crying more than usual and not wanting to be put down.
background: No sick contacts that her parents could identify, no recent travel, no known allergies, fully immunized for her age. She'd had a mild cold about two weeks before all this started, which had seemed to resolve completely before the fever began.

exam.title: General
exam.body: Mia was miserable and irritable, clinging to her mother, with a temperature of 39.7°C that had persisted despite medication. Her hands and feet appeared slightly swollen and reddened.

exam.title: Head and neck
exam.body: Both eyes showed redness without any discharge, her lips were cracked, dry, and deep red, and her tongue had a strikingly bumpy, strawberry-like appearance. A single, firm, swollen lymph node was felt on one side of her neck.

exam.title: Skin
exam.body: A blotchy, red rash covered her trunk and limbs, without the fine, sandpaper-like texture that would point toward a different, more common childhood illness with a similar-looking rash.

investigations.title: Laboratory
investigations.body: Blood was sent to look at her inflammatory markers and to check her heart wasn't being affected:

reports.title: Laboratory Report
lines: White cell count: raised
CRP and ESR: both markedly elevated
Platelets: elevated (a pattern that tends to appear a little later in this kind of illness)
Throat swab: negative for the bacterium responsible for scarlet fever

investigations.title: Imaging
investigations.body: Given the specific concern with this diagnosis for effects on the heart, an echocardiogram was arranged:

reports.title: Imaging Report
lines: Coronary arteries: mildly dilated but no aneurysm formation identified
Heart function: preserved

treatment: Mia was started promptly on an infusion treatment aimed at calming her immune system's overreaction, along with a high dose of a common anti-inflammatory medicine. Within a day of starting treatment, her fever finally broke for good, and over the following days her eyes, lips, and rash all began to settle.
discharge: She was discharged home with a lower daily dose of the same anti-inflammatory medicine to continue for several weeks, and a follow-up echocardiogram booked to make sure her coronary arteries returned fully to normal over time.

title: Couldn't Get Out of Bed
personal: Rachel Kim, 38, Female, 162 cm, 54 kg (recent weight loss), part-time florist. Admitted to the acute medical unit.
incident: For weeks Rachel had felt increasingly exhausted, putting it down to stress and not sleeping well, along with a persistent nausea that had gone off her food entirely and left her several kilograms lighter than usual. This morning she hadn't been able to get out of bed at all, feeling profoundly weak and dizzy the moment she tried to stand, and her husband, worried by how grey she looked, brought her straight in.
background: Rachel mentioned, almost in passing, that her skin had seemed to be getting darker over the past few months in a strange, patchy way, especially in the creases of her palms and around old scars — something she'd assumed was just from the little bit of gardening she still managed to do. No known past medical history, no regular medications, no family history that she was aware of.

exam.title: General
exam.body: Rachel looked profoundly unwell — pale beneath a strange bronzed tint to her skin, particularly noticeable in the folds of her palms, with a blood pressure that dropped sharply from 96 over 60 lying down to 74 over 48 the moment she sat up.

exam.title: Skin
exam.body: Looking more closely at her skin, the doctor found patchy darkening not just in her palm creases but also along her gum line and around a childhood scar on her knee — an unusual and specific pattern of pigmentation.

exam.title: Cardiovascular
exam.body: Her heart rate was fast and her pulse felt thin, consistent with how low her blood pressure had dropped, though her heart sounds themselves were otherwise normal.

investigations.title: Laboratory
investigations.body: Blood was sent urgently, including tests specifically aimed at her hormone levels:

reports.title: Laboratory Report
lines: Sodium: low
Potassium: high
Glucose: low
Morning cortisol: very low
Random blood glucose on admission: also low

investigations.title: Laboratory (further hormone testing)
investigations.body: Additional blood was sent to pin down exactly where the problem was originating:

reports.title: Hormone Report
lines: ACTH: markedly elevated (pointing to a problem originating in the adrenal glands themselves rather than higher up)
Thyroid function: normal, arguing against a thyroid cause

treatment: Rachel was started immediately on fluids and a hormone replacement given directly into her vein, alongside close monitoring of her blood sugar and blood pressure. Within hours her blood pressure began climbing steadily, and by the next day she was able to sit up and eat a little breakfast for the first time in what felt like weeks.
discharge: She was discharged on daily replacement hormone tablets that she'll need for life, along with a card and an emergency injection kit to carry with her in case of future crises, and clear education on increasing her dose during illness or times of stress.

title: Yellow Around the Eyes
personal: Linda Osborne, 63, Female, 160 cm, 68 kg, retired seamstress. Admitted to the surgical ward via the emergency department.
incident: It had started three days ago with a dull ache under her right ribs, not unlike indigestion, which she'd tried to manage with antacids from the cupboard. Yesterday a fever set in, with shivering fits so intense her husband said her teeth were chattering, and this morning he noticed her eyes had taken on a distinct yellow tinge that hadn't been there the night before.
background: Linda had a history of gallstones, diagnosed a couple of years ago after an episode of RUQ pain, though she'd declined surgery at the time since the pain had settled and never come back — until now. No alcohol excess, no known liver disease previously, no recent travel or new medications.

exam.title: General
exam.body: Linda looked unwell and jaundiced, with a visible yellow tinge to the whites of her eyes. Her temperature read 39.1°C, her heart rate 110, and her blood pressure sat a little low at 100 over 62.

exam.title: Abdominal
exam.body: Pressing under her right ribs brought clear tenderness, though without the sharp catching of breath sometimes seen with a different gallbladder problem. No mass was felt, and her abdomen elsewhere was soft.

exam.title: Skin/Eyes
exam.body: Beyond the yellowing of her eyes, her skin also showed a subtle yellow undertone, and she mentioned her urine had looked unusually dark over the past day, with her most recent stool looking paler than normal.

investigations.title: Laboratory
investigations.body: Blood was sent to check her liver function and look for signs of a serious underlying infection:

reports.title: Laboratory Report
lines: White cell count: markedly raised
CRP: markedly elevated
Bilirubin: significantly raised
ALP and GGT: significantly raised, suggesting an obstruction to bile flow
ALT/AST: mildly raised
Blood cultures: sent

investigations.title: Imaging
investigations.body: An ultrasound was followed by a more detailed scan of the bile ducts:

reports.title: Imaging Report
lines: Gallbladder: stones present
Common bile duct: dilated
A stone visualized within the lower portion of the bile duct on the follow-up scan

treatment: Linda was started immediately on intravenous antibiotics and fluids, and once stable enough, taken for a procedure using a scope passed down through her stomach. Her fever and shivering settled within a day of the procedure, and the yellow tinge in her eyes began to fade over the following days.
discharge: Once she'd recovered from the acute infection, Linda was scheduled for removal of her gallbladder during the same admission to prevent this from happening again, and went home a few days later with her jaundice almost entirely resolved and clear advice about the surgery's aftercare.

title: The Leg That Got Worse by the Hour
personal: Douglas Farrow, 55, Male, 178 cm, 102 kg, warehouse worker. Admitted to intensive care via emergency surgery.
incident: It had started two days ago as a small graze on his shin from bumping into a pallet at work, barely worth mentioning at the time. By last night the area had become intensely painful — far more painful, his wife noted, than a scrape that size had any right to be — and by this morning the skin around it had darkened, with the pain now radiating well beyond the visible mark and a fever that had climbed steadily through the night.
background: Douglas had type 2 diabetes, not always tightly controlled, and admitted he hadn't thought much of the graze because "it's just a scratch." No prior similar episodes, no known allergies, no recent hospital stays. He mentioned the pain now felt strangely different from the wound itself — a deep, severe ache that seemed disproportionate to how the skin actually looked.

exam.title: General
exam.body: Douglas looked unwell and anxious, sweating despite the cool room, with a temperature of 38.8°C, a racing pulse of 122, and a blood pressure that had started to drop, reading 96 over 58.

exam.title: Local examination
exam.body: The skin around the wound had taken on a dusky, purplish discoloration spreading well beyond the original graze, with some areas showing small blisters, and the pain on gentle palpation was severe and clearly out of proportion to how the skin looked — a red flag doctors are taught never to ignore. The area also felt unusually firm and, on close inspection, made a faint crackling sensation under the fingertips.

exam.title: Vascular
exam.body: Pulses further down the leg were intact and the foot remained warm, arguing against a primarily blood-flow-related problem being the main issue here.

investigations.title: Laboratory
investigations.body: Blood was sent urgently while preparations for emergency surgery began in parallel:

reports.title: Laboratory Report
lines: White cell count: markedly raised
CRP: markedly elevated
Creatine kinase: elevated, suggesting deeper tissue involvement
Lactate: raised
Blood glucose: elevated

investigations.title: Imaging
investigations.body: A quick scan of the leg was obtained on the way to theatre, without delaying surgery for it:

reports.title: Imaging Report
lines: Soft tissue gas visible tracking along the fascial planes of the lower leg

treatment: Douglas was taken to theatre within the hour for urgent surgery, alongside high-dose intravenous antibiotics and close monitoring in intensive care. He required a further planned return to theatre two days later before the wound was gradually allowed to heal and later covered with a skin graft.
discharge: After several weeks in hospital, Douglas was discharged to continue his recovery and physiotherapy as an outpatient, with his diabetes brought under much tighter control during the admission and clear education on treating even small skin injuries seriously from now on.

title: Couldn't Finish a Sentence
personal: Ella Robinson, 9, Female, 132 cm, 30 kg, primary school student with known asthma. Admitted to the pediatric ward.
incident: Ella had come down with a cold three days ago, nothing unusual for her, but today her breathing had grown noticeably harder despite using her regular inhaler more often than normal. By this evening she was struggling to get more than a few words out before having to pause and catch her breath, and her mother, alarmed by how hard she was working just to breathe, brought her straight to hospital rather than waiting for the morning.
background: Ella had been diagnosed with asthma a few years ago, usually well controlled with her regular inhaler, though her mother admitted she'd been a little lax about the daily preventer inhaler over the summer holidays. No known allergies beyond a mild reaction to cats, no smokers in the house, up to date with immunizations, and no previous admissions to hospital for her asthma before tonight.

exam.title: General
exam.body: Ella was sitting upright, visibly working hard to breathe, able to speak only in short phrases before pausing. Her oxygen level read 91% on room air, her heart rate 128, and her respiratory rate 36 breaths a minute.

exam.title: Respiratory
exam.body: Listening to her chest, the doctor heard widespread wheezing throughout both lungs, with reduced air entry at the bases where the wheeze was almost too quiet to hear at all — a worrying sign rather than a reassuring one, since a truly silent chest can mean too little air is moving to make any noise. Visible tugging was seen at her neck and between her ribs with every breath.

exam.title: Cardiovascular
exam.body: Her heart was racing in a regular rhythm, without murmurs, consistent with the effort of breathing and the medication she'd already been given at home.

investigations.title: Laboratory
investigations.body: A blood gas sample was taken given how hard she was working to breathe, along with routine blood tests:

reports.title: Laboratory Report
lines: Blood gas: low oxygen, carbon dioxide levels creeping toward the higher end of normal — a concerning sign in someone breathing this fast
White cell count: mildly raised, in keeping with the preceding viral illness
CRP: only mildly raised

investigations.title: Imaging
investigations.body: A chest X-ray was taken to make sure nothing else was hiding behind the wheeze:

reports.title: Imaging Report
lines: Lungs: hyperinflated, in keeping with an asthma flare
No focal consolidation
No foreign body visible

treatment: Ella was started on back-to-back nebulized treatments to open her airways, along with a course of oral steroids and supplemental oxygen through small tubing under her nose. Over the following few hours her breathing gradually eased, the wheeze became easier to hear clearly again as more air began moving, and by the next morning she was able to talk in full sentences and asked for breakfast.
discharge: She was discharged home on a short course of steroid tablets and a revised asthma action plan, with a strong emphasis from the team on keeping up with her daily preventer inhaler, and a follow-up appointment booked with the asthma nurse to review her technique and triggers.

title: Frozen Mid-Sentence
personal: Dorothy Hayes, 76, Female, 160 cm, 65 kg, retired postal worker. Admitted to the stroke unit.
incident: She'd been having breakfast with her husband when it happened — mid-sentence, her words suddenly came out slurred and jumbled, as if her mouth had forgotten how to form them. He looked up to see the right side of her face had gone slack, drooping in a way he'd never seen before, and when she reached for her teacup her right hand simply couldn't hold it, sending it shattering to the floor. He called an ambulance immediately, and — remembering something a paramedic had once told him — made a careful note of the exact time it had started.
background: Dorothy had longstanding high blood pressure and an irregular heartbeat, for which she took a blood thinner, though her husband admitted she sometimes forgot a dose here and there. She had high cholesterol, had quit smoking fifteen years ago after decades of the habit, and her mother had suffered a stroke in her seventies. No previous episodes like this, no recent head injury.

exam.title: General
exam.body: Dorothy was alert but visibly frustrated by her inability to get words out clearly. Her blood pressure read 178 over 96, her pulse irregular at 92, and a bedside glucose check came back entirely normal.

exam.title: Neurological
exam.body: The doctor found a right-sided facial droop that spared her forehead, a right arm that drifted steadily downward when held out with her eyes closed, and mild weakness in her right leg. Her speech came out in short, effortful, jumbled phrases. Her left side moved and felt entirely normal.

exam.title: Cardiovascular
exam.body: Her pulse was irregularly irregular under the doctor's fingers, confirming her known heart rhythm problem, with no murmurs heard.

investigations.title: Laboratory
investigations.body: Blood was drawn while imaging was arranged urgently in parallel:

reports.title: Laboratory Report
lines: Blood glucose: normal
Clotting level: within the expected range for her current blood thinner dose
Full blood count: normal

investigations.title: Imaging
investigations.body: An urgent CT scan of her head was performed, followed by a scan of the blood vessels supplying the brain:

reports.title: Imaging Report
lines: No evidence of bleeding
Subtle early changes on the left side of the brain, consistent with reduced blood flow
A blockage identified in one of the main arteries supplying that area

treatment: Given how soon after her symptoms began she'd arrived, the team moved quickly to give her emergency medication through a vein, followed by a specialist procedure carried out through one of her blood vessels. Within hours of the procedure, her speech began to clear, and she was able to lift her right arm off the bed on her own for the first time since breakfast.
discharge: Over the following week, Dorothy made a strong recovery with the help of physiotherapy and speech therapy. She was discharged home with her blood thinner dose reviewed and a clearer system agreed with her husband to make sure she never misses one again.

title: The Lunch That Went Wrong
personal: Jordan Blake, 24, Male, 180 cm, 78 kg, software developer. Brought into the resuscitation area.
incident: At a work lunch, within minutes of eating a dish he didn't realize contained peanuts, his lips began to tingle and swell, and hives broke out rapidly across his chest and arms. His throat started to feel tight, making it hard to swallow, and within another few minutes he felt dizzy and increasingly short of breath. A colleague, recognizing what was happening, dug through his bag for the injector pen he carries while someone else called an ambulance.
background: Jordan has had a known peanut allergy since childhood and carries an adrenaline auto-injector, though he admitted he hadn't checked its expiry date in a while and had hesitated to use it at first, hoping the reaction might settle on its own. He'd had mild asthma as a child, well controlled and untreated for years now.

exam.title: General
exam.body: Jordan had widespread hives across his chest, neck, and arms, visible swelling around his lips and eyes, and an audible wheeze that could be heard without even a stethoscope. His blood pressure had dropped to 82 over 50, his heart racing at 128, and he looked frightened and increasingly breathless.

exam.title: Respiratory
exam.body: Wheeze was heard throughout both lungs, along with a harsher, higher-pitched sound coming from his upper airway, and his air entry was noticeably reduced overall.

exam.title: Skin
exam.body: Raised, red, intensely itchy welts had spread across his trunk and both arms, consistent with a widespread allergic reaction rather than a localized one.

investigations.title: Laboratory
investigations.body: Blood was sent once he'd been stabilized, to confirm the severity of what had happened:

reports.title: Laboratory Report
lines: Serum tryptase (drawn shortly after the reaction): elevated, supporting a significant allergic reaction
Routine bloods: otherwise unremarkable

reports.title: Allergy Report
lines: Skin prick testing: strongly positive to peanut

treatment: Jordan was given an injection into his thigh muscle without delay, along with oxygen, fluids through a drip, and additional medication to calm the reaction and bring down the swelling. Within minutes his breathing eased noticeably, and over the following hour the swelling in his face and the hives across his skin began to fade.
discharge: He was observed for several hours given the small chance of symptoms returning, then discharged with a new pair of auto-injectors, clear written instructions on early warning signs, and a referral to an allergy specialist to review his management plan going forward.

title: Worse Than It Should Be
personal: Sam Whitfield, 19, Male, 182 cm, 76 kg, construction apprentice. Admitted to the orthopedic ward following a leg fracture.
incident: Two hours after having a cast applied for a broken lower leg bone, following a fall from a ladder at work, Sam began complaining of pain that felt far worse than what he'd felt right after the injury itself — pain that the strong medication he'd already been given wasn't touching. He described it as a deep, unrelenting pressure building inside the cast, and mentioned his toes had started to feel numb and tingly, like they'd fallen asleep and wouldn't wake up.
background: No significant past medical history. The fracture had happened a few hours earlier, initially assessed and treated as a straightforward break with no other injuries noted at the time.

exam.title: General
exam.body: Sam was anxious and clearly in severe pain, his heart rate up at 108 and his blood pressure mildly elevated, with a normal temperature.

exam.title: Limb examination
exam.body: The cast was loosened and removed to allow a proper look. The lower leg was tensely swollen and firm to touch, and passively stretching his toes brought a dramatic surge in his pain — far more than would be expected from stretching alone. Sensation over the top of his foot was reduced compared with the other side, and his pulses, though still present, felt fainter than on the uninjured leg.

investigations.title: Compartment Pressure
investigations.body: Given how time-critical this diagnosis is, the surgical team relied heavily on what they'd found on examination, but a fine needle was used to directly measure the pressure inside the muscle compartment of his leg:

reports.title: Compartment Pressure Report
lines: Pressure within the affected compartment: significantly elevated, consistent with critically reduced blood flow to the muscles and nerves inside

investigations.title: Laboratory
investigations.body: Blood was sent to check for early muscle breakdown:

reports.title: Laboratory Report
lines: Creatine kinase: mildly elevated, consistent with early muscle strain from the pressure
Kidney function: normal at this stage

treatment: Sam was taken to theatre without delay for a procedure to make long incisions along the leg, releasing the built-up pressure immediately. The wounds were left open initially and monitored closely, then gradually closed over the following days as the swelling went down.
discharge: He completed his recovery over the following weeks with regular wound checks and physiotherapy to regain strength and movement in his foot, with the team relieved the pressure had been caught and treated before any lasting nerve or muscle damage could set in.

title: A Week Since the Fall
personal: Bernard Wycliffe, 81, Male, 168 cm, 74 kg, retired postmaster. Admitted to the neurology ward.
incident: About a week ago, he'd had a minor fall in his kitchen, bumping his head on the edge of a cupboard, and had seemed fine afterward — brushing it off as nothing more than a bit of a bruise.
