lines: Widespread swelling and fluid collection across both sides of the floor of the mouth and upper neck, tracking down from an infected lower molar tooth
No single large abscess pocket suitable for simple drainage alone

treatment: With his airway secured, Marcus was taken to theatre for the maxillofacial team to surgically drain and wash out the infected area thoroughly, alongside a course of high-dose intravenous antibiotics. His swelling gradually began to reduce over the following days, and his breathing and swallowing steadily improved.
discharge: He was discharged after completing his antibiotic course, with a firm and detailed conversation about the importance of regular dental care going forward, given how close a simple untreated tooth infection had come to threatening his airway.

title: Repeating the Same Sentence
personal: Fiona Marsh, 30, Female, 165 cm, 63 kg, primary school teacher. Admitted to the neurology intensive care unit.
incident: For two days she'd had what seemed like a bad flu, with fever and headache, but this morning her partner noticed she was behaving strangely — repeating the same phrases, unable to recall simple recent events, and at one point staring blankly for almost a minute before seeming confused about where she was. An hour before arriving at hospital, she had a brief episode of jerking movements on her right side that lasted less than a minute.
background: No significant past medical history, no recent travel, no known cold sores or other herpes-related symptoms that she or her partner could recall, no illicit drug use, no recent vaccinations.

exam.title: General
exam.body: Fiona was drowsy but rousable, temperature 38.7°C, heart rate 104, blood pressure normal.

exam.title: Neurological
exam.body: She was confused, disoriented to time and place, with mild weakness noted in her right arm and leg that hadn't been present according to her partner before today, and difficulty finding the right words when trying to speak.

exam.title: Skin/ENT
exam.body: No rash anywhere on her body, no neck stiffness on gentle testing, no cold sores or blisters visible around her mouth.

investigations.title: Imaging
investigations.body: An urgent MRI scan of her brain was arranged:

reports.title: Imaging Report
lines: Areas of swelling and abnormal signal within the temporal lobes on both sides, a pattern strongly associated with one particular viral cause of brain inflammation

investigations.title: Laboratory
investigations.body: A lumbar puncture was performed to sample the fluid around her brain:

reports.title: Laboratory Report
lines: CSF white cell count: raised, predominantly lymphocytes
CSF protein: mildly raised
A specific viral genetic test on the fluid: positive for the herpes simplex virus

treatment: Fiona was started on a targeted medication through a vein without waiting for the final confirmatory test result, since early treatment makes a real difference to outcomes. She was also given medication to prevent further seizures and monitored closely in intensive care. Over the following days, her confusion and speech difficulty began to improve, and the right-sided weakness gradually lessened.
discharge: She completed a full course of antiviral treatment in hospital, with ongoing rehabilitation arranged for some residual difficulties with memory and word-finding, and follow-up scans planned to monitor her recovery over the following months.

title: Too Breathless for the Kitchen
personal: Sandra Michaels, 33, Female, 162 cm, 74 kg, three weeks postpartum with her third child. Admitted to the cardiology ward.
incident: For the past week she'd felt increasingly breathless, initially putting it down to the usual exhaustion of caring for a newborn along with two older children. Over the past two days she's found herself unable to lie flat without feeling like she couldn't breathe, waking up gasping in the night and needing to prop herself up with extra pillows. Today she noticed her ankles had become visibly swollen, and even walking to the kitchen left her breathless and lightheaded.
background: An uncomplicated pregnancy and vaginal delivery three weeks ago, no previous heart problems, no high blood pressure during this or previous pregnancies, no smoking, this being her third child with no similar symptoms after the first two.

exam.title: General
exam.body: Sandra was breathless even at rest, unable to lie flat comfortably. Blood pressure 108 over 70, heart rate 108, oxygen saturation mildly reduced at 94%.

exam.title: Cardiovascular
exam.body: The veins in her neck were visibly distended, a soft murmur was heard that hadn't been documented before her pregnancy, and an extra heart sound was noted that doctors specifically listen for when heart failure is suspected.

exam.title: Respiratory
exam.body: Fine crackling sounds were heard at the bases of both lungs, consistent with fluid backing up into the lungs from a struggling heart.

exam.title: Peripheral
exam.body: Swelling was noted over both ankles, pitting when pressed with a finger.

reports.title: Laboratory Report
lines: A specific marker of heart strain (BNP): markedly elevated
D-dimer: mildly raised, as can happen normally around the time of pregnancy, making it less specifically useful here
Hemoglobin: normal, arguing against significant postpartum blood loss as the cause

investigations.title: Imaging
investigations.body: An urgent echocardiogram was performed:

reports.title: Imaging Report
lines: The main pumping chamber of the heart significantly enlarged and weakened
Overall pumping function markedly reduced compared with what would be expected
No evidence of a structural problem present before her pregnancy

treatment: Sandra was started on a combination of heart medications carefully chosen to be compatible with breastfeeding, along with fluid restriction and close monitoring of her breathing and fluid balance. Over the following week, her breathlessness gradually eased, she was able to lie flat again without difficulty, and the swelling in her ankles reduced.
discharge: She was discharged home on ongoing heart medication with close cardiology follow-up and a repeat echocardiogram planned in a few months to check how much her heart function had recovered, along with support arranged at home given the demands of caring for a newborn while managing a new heart condition.

title: A Curtain From the Edge
personal: Peter Nguyen, 55, Male, 173 cm, 80 kg, accountant. Admitted to the ophthalmology ward.
incident: Over the past two days he's noticed an increasing number of small, dark specks drifting across his vision in his right eye, along with brief flashes of light at the edge of his vision on that side, particularly noticeable in a dark room. This morning, he described a dark curtain or shadow that seemed to be creeping in from the outer edge of his vision on the right side, now covering roughly the upper part of what he can see out of that eye.
background: He's been significantly nearsighted since his twenties, wearing strong glasses, no previous eye surgery, no recent trauma to the eye that he recalls, though he mentions bumping his head lightly on a cupboard door about a week ago that he hadn't thought was serious at the time.

exam.title: General
exam.body: Peter was otherwise well, with no pain reported in the eye itself, and normal vital signs.

exam.title: Eye examination — visual fields
exam.body: A clear area of visual field loss was mapped out in the upper portion of his right eye's vision, corresponding to what he'd described as a curtain effect.

exam.title: Eye examination — back of the eye
exam.body: Using specialized equipment to look at the back of his eye, the retina was seen to be lifted away from its normal position in the affected area, with a small tear visible at its edge.

investigations.title: Eye Examination
investigations.body: A detailed examination of the back of the eye using specialized lenses and equipment, performed by the ophthalmology team, was the key test in this case:

reports.title: Eye Examination Report
lines: A retinal tear identified with associated detachment of the retina in the upper portion of the right eye, threatening to extend toward the central area of vision if left untreated

investigations.title: Imaging
investigations.body: An ultrasound scan of the eye was also performed to fully map the extent of the detachment:

reports.title: Imaging Report
lines: Confirmed the area of retinal detachment
Ruled out any bleeding within the eye that might have obscured the view during direct examination

treatment: Given how urgently this needed addressing before it could threaten his central vision permanently, Peter was taken to theatre the same day for an eye operation. He was advised to keep his head in a specific position for several days afterward to help it heal.
discharge: He was discharged with clear instructions on positioning and activity restrictions during his recovery, along with close ophthalmology follow-up to monitor how well the retina was healing back into place, and advice on the warning signs to watch for in his other eye given his risk factors.

title: The Room Spun Before She Fell
personal: Joan Whitaker, 70, Female, 160 cm, 68 kg, retired librarian. Admitted to the neurosurgical intensive care unit.
incident: While getting up from her armchair to answer the door, Joan suddenly felt the room spin violently around her, lost her balance, and fell back into the chair rather than making it to the door at all. Within minutes she developed a severe headache at the back of her head, along with repeated vomiting, and her daughter, arriving moments later, found her unable to sit up straight without listing to one side, her speech sounding slurred though the words themselves made sense.
background: Longstanding high blood pressure, not always taken consistently according to her daughter, no previous strokes, no blood thinners, no recent falls or head injury before today.

exam.title: General
exam.body: Joan was alert but clearly unwell, blood pressure 198 over 108, heart rate 78, vomiting once more during the assessment.

exam.title: Neurological — cerebellar signs
exam.body: She was unable to sit upright without support, listing to the left, with marked incoordination noted when asked to touch her nose then the doctor's finger repeatedly with her left hand, and her speech had a slurred, poorly coordinated quality rather than the specific pattern seen with a problem affecting language itself.

exam.title: Neurological — other
exam.body: Her limb strength was preserved on formal testing despite the incoordination, pupils were equal and reactive, and there was no facial droop.

investigations.title: Imaging
investigations.body: An urgent CT scan of her head was performed:

reports.title: Imaging Report
lines: A collection of blood within the cerebellum, with early signs of pressure building on the nearby fluid spaces of the brain — a situation doctors watch extremely closely given how quickly it can worsen in this particular location

reports.title: Laboratory Report
lines: Clotting screen: normal, no blood thinner effect detected
Full blood count: normal

treatment: Given the early signs of pressure building, the neurosurgical team took Joan to theatre to relieve it before it could worsen further. Her blood pressure was also carefully controlled throughout her recovery. Over the following days, her balance and coordination began to improve steadily with the help of physiotherapy.
discharge: She was discharged to a rehabilitation unit to continue building her strength and coordination, with her blood pressure medication reviewed and a much stricter plan put in place to make sure she takes it consistently going forward.

title: Ten Days In
personal: Baby Grayson Miller, 10 days old (born at 28 weeks gestation), Male, 38 cm, 1.1 kg, premature infant. Admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit.
incident: Grayson had been slowly progressing with his feeds over his first ten days of life in the neonatal unit, tolerating small increasing volumes of milk. Overnight, the nursing staff noticed his abdomen had become visibly more distended than usual, and he'd started bringing back green-tinged milk after his feeds rather than tolerating them as before. By the early morning, a small amount of blood was noticed in his nappy, and he'd become noticeably less active, with several brief pauses in his breathing that needed gentle stimulation to correct.
background: Born at 28 weeks due to his mother's pregnancy complications, otherwise following a fairly typical course for a baby born this early, on slowly increasing volumes of breast milk feeds, no known infections previously, umbilical line removed a few days ago without complication.

exam.title: General
exam.body: Grayson was lethargic compared with his usual activity level, temperature unstable (fluctuating rather than a clear fever), several brief pauses in breathing noted on the monitor, heart rate mildly elevated.

exam.title: Abdominal
exam.body: His abdomen was visibly distended and shiny-looking, with the skin over it appearing slightly discolored in patches, and the doctor could feel it was firmer to gentle palpation than it had been on previous days.

exam.title: Overall clinical picture
exam.body: Pale, poor peripheral circulation with cool hands and feet, and reduced responsiveness to handling compared with his usual behavior.

investigations.title: Imaging
investigations.body: An abdominal X-ray was taken urgently, a key test for exactly this situation:

reports.title: Imaging Report
lines: Gas visible within the wall of the bowel itself, a finding specific to this condition and not seen in ordinary feed intolerance
No free air outside the bowel identified at this point

reports.title: Laboratory Report
lines: White cell count: abnormal, with both very high and very low counts seen in this condition depending on severity
Platelets: reduced
CRP: markedly elevated
Blood gas: showing early signs of the body working hard to compensate for the illness

treatment: Grayson's feeds were stopped completely to rest his bowel, and a tube was placed to gently decompress his stomach while he was supported entirely through a vein for nutrition, alongside a course of antibiotics and extremely close monitoring by the neonatal team, with repeat abdominal X-rays taken regularly. Thankfully, over the following week, his abdomen gradually became less distended, and the concerning findings on his X-rays slowly resolved without needing surgery.
discharge: Feeds were reintroduced very gradually and cautiously over the following couple of weeks once he'd fully recovered, with the neonatal team keeping him under close observation throughout the rest of his stay before he was eventually well enough, weeks later, to go home with his family.

title: A Crackling Under the Skin
personal: Anthony Ricci, 50, Male, 176 cm, 90 kg, sales representative. Admitted to the general surgical ward via the emergency department.
incident: After a heavy meal and several drinks at a work dinner, Anthony began vomiting forcefully and repeatedly. During one particularly violent episode, he felt a sudden, severe tearing pain in his chest and upper abdomen that made him cry out, unlike anything he'd felt with the vomiting itself, and within the hour he'd become increasingly breathless and noticed a strange crackling sensation when he pressed on the skin of his neck and upper chest.
background: No significant past medical history, occasional heavy drinking at social events, no previous similar episodes, no known ulcers or swallowing problems before tonight.

exam.title: General
exam.body: Anthony was unwell and distressed, breathing rapidly. Temperature 38.3°C, heart rate 122, blood pressure 98 over 60.

exam.title: Chest/Neck
exam.body: Gently pressing on the skin over his neck and upper chest produced a distinctive crackling sensation under the fingertips, caused by air that had escaped into the tissues beneath the skin — a finding doctors take very seriously as a specific clue pointing toward a hole somewhere in the airway or gullet.

exam.title: Cardiovascular
exam.body: Heart sounds were somewhat distant and muffled, though rhythm was regular, with no clear murmur.

exam.title: Abdominal
exam.body: Mild tenderness in the upper abdomen, without the widespread rigidity that might be seen with a different kind of perforation lower down.

investigations.title: Imaging
investigations.body: A chest X-ray was taken first, followed by a specific scan using a swallowed contrast material to look directly for a leak:

reports.title: Imaging Report
lines: Air visible within the tissues of the chest wall and around the gullet
Contrast swallow study confirmed contrast leaking out from a tear in the wall of the esophagus into the surrounding chest cavity

reports.title: Laboratory Report
lines: White cell count: markedly raised
CRP: markedly elevated
Troponin: normal, arguing against a heart attack as the cause of his pain

treatment: Anthony was taken to theatre urgently for the surgical team to repair the damage and thoroughly wash out the chest cavity, given how quickly leaking contents can cause serious infection. He was kept without anything by mouth for an extended period afterward, fed entirely through a tube bypassing the repair site while it healed, alongside a prolonged course of antibiotics.
discharge: After a lengthy recovery in hospital with the repair confirmed to be healing well on a follow-up contrast study, he was gradually reintroduced to eating and discharged home, with clear advice about avoiding forceful vomiting where possible in the future and seeking urgent help immediately if anything like this chest pain ever happened again.

title: A Gasp at the End of the Cough
personal: Baby Ivy Chen, 6 weeks, Female, 55 cm, 4.8 kg, infant. Admitted to the pediatric ward.
incident: For the past week Ivy has had a mild runny nose and occasional cough that her parents assumed was an ordinary baby cold. Over the past two days, though, the cough has changed character dramatically, coming in sudden, intense bursts that leave her red-faced and struggling, followed on a few occasions by a high-pitched gasping sound as she finally manages to draw breath back in. Twice today, after a coughing fit, she briefly stopped breathing altogether for a few seconds before starting again on her own, which terrified her parents into bringing her straight in.
background: Born full term, too young yet for her first scheduled whooping cough vaccination, her mother did not receive the vaccine during this pregnancy, no other significant medical history, older sibling at home had a "cold" with a lingering cough for the past few weeks that never resolved fully.

exam.title: General
exam.body: Ivy was alert and interactive between coughing episodes, though appearing exhausted. Temperature normal, oxygen saturation dipping notably during and immediately after coughing fits before recovering.

exam.title: Respiratory
exam.body: Between episodes, her chest was clear with normal breath sounds; during a witnessed coughing fit, however, a distinctive high-pitched gasping sound was heard as she tried to breathe in at the end of the coughing burst, and her color briefly dusky before recovering.

exam.title: ENT/General
exam.body: No fever, no drooling, no signs of an upper airway obstruction from another cause, and her weight gain since birth had been appropriate for her age.

investigations.title: Laboratory
investigations.body: A swab from the back of her nose and throat was sent for a specific test:

reports.title: Laboratory Report
lines: A specific genetic test on the nasopharyngeal swab: positive for the bacterium responsible for whooping cough

reports.title: Laboratory Report
lines: White cell count notably showed a very high proportion of one particular type of white blood cell, a pattern classically associated with this specific infection in young infants

treatment: Ivy was admitted for close monitoring given her age and the concerning pauses in breathing, with oxygen support available during and after coughing fits, and a course of antibiotics started both to help her own recovery and to reduce how contagious she was to others. Nursing staff kept her under continuous monitoring to catch and respond quickly to any breathing pauses, which gradually became less frequent over the following several days.
discharge: She was discharged home once her breathing pauses had settled and her parents felt confident managing her ongoing cough, which the team explained could linger for several more weeks even after treatment, along with advice on keeping her away from other infants where possible and making sure the rest of the household, including her older sibling, were checked and treated if needed.

title: The Cough Changed Color
personal: Gordon Price, 68, Male, 172 cm, 78 kg, retired factory worker, longtime smoker. Admitted to the respiratory ward.
incident: Over the past three days his usual morning cough had gotten markedly worse, bringing up much more phlegm than normal and changing color from its usual clear-white to a thick yellow-green. His breathlessness, ordinarily manageable with his regular inhalers, had progressively worsened until today even getting dressed left him gasping, and he'd started using the muscles in his neck just to breathe.
background: Diagnosed with COPD five years ago, on regular inhalers, smoked heavily for over forty years though cut down significantly in recent years. Two previous hospital admissions for similar flare-ups, no known heart problems, flu vaccine received this year.

exam.title: General
exam.body: Gordon was visibly working hard to breathe, using accessory neck muscles, pursed-lip breathing. Respiratory rate 26, oxygen saturation 88% on room air, temperature 37.4°C.

exam.title: Respiratory
exam.body: Widespread wheeze was heard throughout both lungs with a prolonged breathing-out phase, reduced air entry generally rather than in one specific area, no focal crackles to suggest a localized chest infection.

exam.title: Cardiovascular
exam.body: Heart sounds were difficult to hear clearly over the noisy breathing, no obvious ankle swelling, no raised neck veins.

reports.title: Laboratory Report
lines: Arterial blood gas: low oxygen with a mildly raised carbon dioxide level, in keeping with his condition
White cell count: mildly raised
CRP: mildly elevated

reports.title: Imaging Report
lines: Hyperinflated lungs consistent with his underlying condition
No focal consolidation to suggest pneumonia
No pneumothorax

treatment: Gordon was started on nebulized medication to open his airways, a short course of oral steroids, controlled oxygen therapy carefully titrated given his tendency to retain carbon dioxide, and antibiotics given the change in his sputum. Over the following two days, his breathing gradually eased and his oxygen levels improved on lower amounts of supplemental oxygen.
discharge: He was discharged with a course of steroids and antibiotics to complete at home, a review of his inhaler technique, and a referral to the respiratory team for consideration of a pulmonary rehabilitation program to help him manage his condition longer term.

title: Sleeping Upright
personal: Walter Higgins, 75, Male, 175 cm, 90 kg, retired bank manager, known heart failure. Admitted to the cardiology ward.
incident: Over the past week he's noticed his ankles swelling more than usual and his weight creeping up despite no change in his eating habits, and today he woke up feeling as though he couldn't get enough air, needing to sit bolt upright in bed to breathe comfortably. His wife mentioned he'd been coughing up small amounts of frothy, pale phlegm overnight, and he'd found himself unable to manage even his usual short walk to the mailbox without stopping to catch his breath.
background: Diagnosed with heart failure four years ago following a heart attack, on regular heart medications though he admits he ran out of his water tablet a few days ago and hadn't gotten around to refilling it. No recent chest pain, eats a diet he acknowledges is "saltier than it should be."

exam.title: General
exam.body: Walter was breathless sitting upright, unable to lie flat. Respiratory rate 24, oxygen saturation 90% on room air, weight up several kilograms from his last recorded weight.

exam.title: Cardiovascular
exam.body: The veins in his neck were visibly raised, a third heart sound was heard — a specific finding doctors listen for in this condition — and his heart rate was mildly elevated.

exam.title: Respiratory
exam.body: Fine crackling sounds were heard throughout both lung bases, consistent with fluid in the lungs.

exam.title: Peripheral
exam.body: Both ankles and lower legs showed significant pitting swelling extending partway up his shins.

reports.title: Laboratory Report
lines: A specific marker of heart strain (BNP): markedly elevated
Kidney function: mildly impaired
Electrolytes: sodium mildly low

reports.title: Imaging Report
lines: Fluid visible at the base of both lungs
Enlarged heart shadow
Prominent markings consistent with fluid backing up through the lung's blood vessels

treatment: Walter was given intravenous medication to help his body remove the excess fluid, along with careful monitoring of his weight, fluid balance, and kidney function each day, and his regular heart medications were restarted and optimized. Over the following four days, the swelling in his legs reduced substantially, his breathing became much easier, and he was able to lie flat comfortably again at night.
discharge: He was discharged on an adjusted medication regimen with clear instructions on daily weighing and salt restriction, along with a heart failure nurse arranged to follow up closely at home and make sure he never runs out of his medications again.

title: Trying to Jump Out
personal: Linda Barrett, 60, Female, 162 cm, 70 kg, part-time bookkeeper. Admitted to the cardiology assessment unit.
incident: While doing housework this afternoon, Linda suddenly felt her heart racing and fluttering in her chest, a sensation she described as her heart "trying to jump out," accompanied by lightheadedness and a mild shortness of breath that made her sit down immediately. The sensation didn't settle after resting for twenty minutes as it usually might with ordinary anxiety, prompting her husband to bring her in.
background: No previous heart problems diagnosed, mild high blood pressure not currently on treatment, drinks a moderate amount of coffee daily, had a few glasses of wine at a dinner party the night before, no known thyroid problems, no prior similar episodes that she can recall clearly.

exam.title: General
exam.body: Linda was anxious but alert. Blood pressure 128 over 82, respiratory rate 18, otherwise comfortable at rest once seated.

exam.title: Cardiovascular
exam.body: Her pulse was rapid and irregularly irregular, with no clear pattern to the spacing between beats, heart rate around 140, no murmurs heard.

exam.title: Neck/Thyroid
exam.body: No goiter or thyroid enlargement felt, no tremor.

investigations.title: ECG
investigations.body: A tracing of her heart's electrical activity was taken:

reports.title: ECG Report
lines: An irregularly irregular rhythm with no clear, organized P waves visible before each heartbeat, and a rapid overall heart rate, consistent with the suspected rhythm disturbance

reports.title: Laboratory Report
lines: Thyroid function: normal, arguing against an overactive thyroid as the trigger
Electrolytes: normal
Full blood count: normal, arguing against anemia as a cause

treatment: Linda was given medication through a vein to slow her heart rate down to a safer, more comfortable range, with continuous heart monitoring throughout. Within a couple of hours her heart rate settled into a more controlled range, and though the underlying rhythm problem persisted on the monitor, her symptoms of racing and breathlessness resolved considerably.
discharge: She was discharged on a regular heart-rate-controlling medication and a blood thinner to reduce her risk of stroke associated with this rhythm, with cardiology follow-up arranged to discuss longer-term options, including whether attempting to restore a normal rhythm might be appropriate for her.
dd1: Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response
final: Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response

title: Small Amounts, Often
personal: Chloe Hartman, 26, Female, 165 cm, 61 kg, marketing assistant. Seen in the same-day clinic.
incident: For the past day and a half she's had a burning sensation every time she urinates, along with a frequent, urgent need to go despite passing only small amounts each time, and this morning she noticed her urine looked cloudier and smelled stronger than usual. Aside from mild discomfort low in her pelvis, she otherwise feels well in herself, without any fevers or back pain.
background: Has had two similar episodes in the past couple of years, both resolved quickly with a short course of antibiotics. Sexually active with a regular partner, no known kidney problems, not currently pregnant, drinks relatively little water during busy workdays by her own admission.

exam.title: General
exam.body: Chloe was well-looking, comfortable, afebrile, with normal vital signs.

exam.title: Abdominal
exam.body: Mild suprapubic tenderness only, no tenderness over either kidney area in her back, no rebound or guarding.

exam.title: General, further
exam.body: No vaginal discharge reported or seen, no rash, no joint symptoms.

reports.title: Laboratory Report
lines: Urine dipstick: positive for leukocytes and nitrites, small amount of blood
Urine culture: sent to confirm the specific bacterium and check antibiotic sensitivity

reports.title: Follow-up Note
lines: Symptoms expected to improve within 48 hours of starting treatment
Return advised if fever or back pain developed, which would suggest the infection had spread to the kidneys

treatment: Chloe was started on a short course of oral antibiotics along with simple pain relief for the discomfort, and advised to drink plenty of fluids to help flush her system. Her symptoms began improving within a day of starting the antibiotics, with the burning and urgency settling steadily.
discharge: She completed her short course of antibiotics with symptoms fully resolved, and was given general advice on staying well hydrated and urinating after intercourse, which can help reduce how often these infections recur.

title: A Shimmer at the Edge
personal: Emma Whitfield, 32, Female, 168 cm, 64 kg, graphic designer. Seen in the emergency department observation area.
incident: She woke this morning with a throbbing, one-sided headache on the right side of her head that had been building in intensity over the past hour, accompanied by nausea and a strong aversion to the bright light in her bedroom. About twenty minutes before the headache started, she'd noticed a strange shimmering, zigzag pattern appear at the edge of her vision that slowly spread and then faded on its own before the pain began.
background: Has had similar headaches on and off since her teenage years, roughly once or twice a month, often around her period or during stressful weeks at work. Her mother has a history of "bad migraines" too, no recent head injury, no fever, no neck stiffness.

exam.title: General
exam.body: Emma was uncomfortable, keeping her eyes closed against the light, otherwise well, afebrile, with normal vital signs.

exam.title: Neurological
exam.body: Fully alert and oriented, no neck stiffness, no weakness or sensory changes anywhere, normal reflexes, pupils equal and reactive.

exam.title: General, further
exam.body: No rash, no recent illness, headache pattern and associated visual disturbance closely matching her previous, well-documented episodes.

investigations.title: Clinical
investigations.body: Given how classic and consistent this presentation was with her known history, and the entirely normal neurological examination, the priority was simply confirming there were no worrying features:

reports.title: Clinical Assessment Report
lines: No red-flag features identified (no sudden "thunderclap" onset, no fever, no neurological deficit, no first-ever severe headache in someone over 50), supporting a primary headache disorder rather than a more serious underlying cause

reports.title: Observation Report
lines: Blood pressure and other vital signs entirely normal throughout her stay

treatment: Emma was given targeted headache medication along with anti-sickness medication and encouraged to rest in a quiet, dark room. Within a couple of hours, her headache had eased substantially and the nausea settled.
discharge: She was discharged with medication to keep on hand for future attacks, advice on identifying and managing her personal triggers, and a suggestion to discuss preventive treatment with her regular doctor given how frequently these headaches have been affecting her.

title: Even the Sheet Hurt
personal: Brian Sutcliffe, 55, Male, 178 cm, 96 kg, sales manager. Admitted to the acute medical unit for pain control.
incident: He went to bed feeling entirely fine, but woke in the early hours of the morning with sudden, excruciating pain in his right big toe, so severe that even the weight of the bedsheet touching it was unbearable. By morning, the toe had become visibly red, swollen, and shiny-looking, and he found himself unable to put any weight on that foot at all.
background: Enjoys red meat and beer regularly, a family history of "bad joints" on his father's side, no previous episodes quite this severe though he recalls a milder, similar ache in the same toe a couple of years ago that settled on its own within a few days. No known kidney problems, no recent injury to the toe.

exam.title: General
exam.body: Brian was otherwise well, mildly uncomfortable from the pain, temperature 37.6°C, normal blood pressure and heart rate.

exam.title: Joint examination
exam.body: The big toe joint on the right was markedly swollen, hot, and intensely red, shiny-looking skin stretched over it, with any attempted movement of the joint causing severe pain; no wound or break in the skin to suggest an entry point for infection.

investigations.title: Laboratory
investigations.body: Blood was sent, along with fluid drawn from the joint itself given the concern for infection:

reports.title: Laboratory Report
lines: Serum uric acid level: elevated
White cell count: mildly raised
CRP: mildly elevated
Joint fluid under polarized light: needle-shaped crystals identified, confirming the specific type of crystal responsible for this condition
Joint fluid Gram stain and culture: no bacteria seen or grown, arguing against a joint infection

reports.title: Imaging Report
lines: Soft tissue swelling around the joint, no fracture, no bony changes

treatment: Brian was started on a strong anti-inflammatory medication to bring the pain and swelling under control quickly, with his toe rested and elevated. Within two days, the redness and swelling had noticeably reduced, and he was able to gradually start putting weight back on the foot.
discharge: He was discharged with advice on dietary changes to reduce his risk of future flares, along with a discussion about starting a long-term medication to lower his uric acid levels given how significant this episode had been, and a plan to follow up with his regular doctor to monitor his levels going forward.

title: Spreading From the Scrape
personal: Nathan Ross, 47, Male, 180 cm, 95 kg, warehouse supervisor. Admitted to the acute medical unit.
incident: Three days ago he scraped his shin on a metal shelf at work, cleaned it up himself, and thought nothing more of it. Over the past two days, though, the skin around the scrape has become increasingly red, warm, and swollen, with the redness clearly spreading outward from the original scrape, and today he developed a mild fever and felt generally unwell and achy.
background: Type 2 diabetes reasonably well controlled with tablets, no known allergies, no previous episodes of skin infection like this, works on his feet most of the day in a warehouse environment.

exam.title: General
exam.body: Nathan was mildly unwell, temperature 38.0°C, heart rate 96, otherwise stable.

exam.title: Limb examination
exam.body: A clearly demarcated area of redness, warmth, and swelling was seen spreading from the original scrape on his shin, tender to touch but without the severe, out-of-proportion pain, skin discoloration, or crackling sensation that would raise concern for a much more dangerous, deeper infection. Pulses in the foot were normal and easily felt.

reports.title: Laboratory Report
lines: White cell count: mildly raised
CRP: mildly elevated
Blood cultures: sent as a precaution

investigations.title: Monitoring
investigations.body: A mark was drawn around the edge of the redness to track whether it was spreading further despite treatment:

reports.title: Monitoring Report
lines: The marked border was checked again the following day and had not extended beyond the original line, suggesting the infection was responding to treatment rather than progressing

treatment: Nathan was started on a course of antibiotics targeting the bacteria most commonly responsible for this kind of skin infection, with his leg elevated to help reduce the swelling, and his blood sugar levels monitored closely given his diabetes. Over the following three days, the redness and swelling gradually reduced, and his fever settled.
discharge: He completed his course of antibiotics at home, with advice on proper wound care for any future skin injuries and a reminder of how important good blood sugar control is in helping prevent and fight off infections like this one.

title: Hit by a Truck
personal: Karen Douglas, 40, Female, 165 cm, 68 kg, primary school teacher. Seen in the acute assessment unit.
incident: Yesterday she felt perfectly well at work, but woke this morning with a sudden onset of high fever, severe body aches, a pounding headache, and an overwhelming exhaustion that made even sitting up in bed feel like too much effort. A dry, persistent cough developed through the day, along with a sore throat, and she described feeling "hit by a truck" compared with the more gradual onset of an ordinary cold.
background: Works closely with young children, several of whom have been off school sick recently with "colds and flu." She hasn't had her flu vaccine this year, no chronic health conditions, no known allergies, not pregnant.

exam.title: General
exam.body: Karen was flushed and visibly fatigued. Temperature 39.2°C, heart rate 100, blood pressure normal, appearing generally unwell rather than having a specific focus of illness.

exam.title: Respiratory
exam.body: Chest clear, no crackles or wheeze, no signs of the infection having settled into her lungs.

exam.title: ENT
exam.body: Throat mildly red without the thick white exudate sometimes seen with a specific bacterial throat infection, no swollen glands felt in her neck.

investigations.title: Laboratory
investigations.body: A combined swab from the back of her nose and throat was sent for testing:

reports.title: Laboratory Report
lines: Combined respiratory viral swab: positive for influenza, negative for the virus responsible for COVID-19

reports.title: Laboratory Report
lines: White cell count: normal, in keeping with a viral rather than bacterial illness
CRP: only mildly raised

treatment: Given how early in her illness she'd presented, Karen was started on an antiviral medication aimed at shortening the duration and severity of her symptoms, along with plenty of fluids, rest, and simple medication to manage her fever and aches. Over the following three to four days, her fever gradually settled and her energy slowly began to return.
discharge: She was advised to rest at home until fully recovered and fever-free, with clear guidance on staying away from work and other people while contagious, and a strong recommendation to get her flu vaccine each year going forward given how exposed she is working with young children.

title: Spots at Different Stages
personal: Lily Anderson, 5, Female, 110 cm, 18 kg, kindergartener. Seen in the pediatric assessment unit.
incident: Yesterday Lily developed a mild fever and seemed generally out of sorts, and this morning her mother noticed a handful of small, red, itchy spots had appeared on her chest and back. Over the course of the day, more spots have continued to appear across her body, including her scalp, and some of the earlier ones have started turning into small, fluid-filled blisters that she keeps trying to scratch.
background: Previously healthy, not yet vaccinated against this particular illness since her family had been meaning to schedule it. A classmate at nursery was sent home with "spots" about two weeks ago. No known allergies, otherwise fully immunized for her age.

exam.title: General
exam.body: Lily was mildly unwell but active and playful between bouts of scratching, temperature 38.0°C, otherwise stable.

exam.title: Skin
exam.body: Numerous small red spots, fluid-filled blisters, and crusted-over lesions were seen scattered across her trunk, back, scalp, and face, with lesions at several different stages of development all present at the same time — a pattern doctors specifically recognize as typical of this illness.

exam.title: ENT/General
exam.body: A few small spots were also seen inside her mouth, mild redness of her throat, no significant swelling of her tonsils.

reports.title: Clinical Assessment Report
lines: Lesions in multiple stages of development (spots, blisters, and crusts all present together) across the trunk and scalp — a distribution and pattern specific to this particular viral illness rather than the more limited hands-feet-mouth pattern of the alternative being considered

reports.title: Monitoring Report
lines: Temperature settled with simple fever medication; adequate fluid intake maintained throughout the assessment

treatment: Lily was managed with simple measures at home — fever medication, cool baths, and specific lotion to ease the itching, along with clear advice to keep her fingernails short to reduce skin damage from scratching and lower the risk of the spots becoming infected. Over the following week, the spots gradually crusted over and stopped appearing.
discharge: She was kept off nursery until all the spots had fully crusted over, as advised, and her family was encouraged to arrange her vaccination against this illness for any future, unvaccinated siblings to help prevent it happening again in the household.

title: Spots Inside His Mouth
personal: Oscar Bennett, 4, Male, 105 cm, 17 kg, preschooler. Admitted to the pediatric ward.
incident: Four days ago Oscar developed a fever, along with a runny nose, cough, and red, watery eyes that his mother assumed was just another childhood cold. Yesterday, small white spots appeared inside his mouth, which she hadn't seen before with any of his previous colds, and today a blotchy red rash has started spreading down from his face and behind his ears onto his neck and chest, with his fever climbing higher rather than settling.
background: Unvaccinated against this illness, as his parents had chosen to delay and then never rescheduled his routine vaccinations. Recently returned from a family holiday abroad where an outbreak of this illness had been reported in the area they visited. No other significant medical history.

exam.title: General
exam.body: Oscar was miserable and lethargic, temperature 39.5°C, red, watery eyes sensitive to light, persistent cough.

exam.title: ENT/Mouth
exam.body: Small white spots with a red base were seen on the inside of his cheeks, a finding specifically associated with this illness and typically appearing just before the skin rash.

exam.title: Skin
exam.body: A blotchy, red, slightly raised rash was seen starting behind his ears and along his hairline, spreading down onto his face, neck, and upper chest, in a pattern that spreads gradually downward over several days.

investigations.title: Laboratory
investigations.body: Blood and a throat/nose swab were sent to confirm the specific virus:

reports.title: Laboratory Report
lines: Measles-specific antibody testing: positive
Throat swab: positive for measles virus on genetic testing

reports.title: Laboratory Report
lines: White cell count: reduced, a pattern often seen with this particular viral illness
CRP: only mildly raised, without evidence yet of a secondary bacterial infection

treatment: Oscar was managed with supportive care, including fever medication, fluids to keep him well hydrated, and close monitoring for any signs of the complications this illness can occasionally cause, such as chest or ear infections. Public health authorities were also notified given how contagious this illness is. Over the following several days, his fever gradually settled and the rash began to fade, working its way down his body in the same order it had appeared.
discharge: He was kept isolated until no longer considered contagious, and his family had a detailed conversation with the pediatric team about catching up on his full vaccination schedule to protect him and others going forward.

title: Spots on Her Palms and Soles
personal: Ruby Chan, 3, Female, 96 cm, 15 kg, nursery attendee. Seen in the pediatric assessment unit.
incident: Two days ago Ruby developed a mild fever and started refusing her food, which her parents initially put down to teething or a minor bug. Yesterday, small sores appeared inside her mouth, making her reluctant to eat or drink anything at all, and today small red spots and blisters have appeared on both her palms and the soles of her feet, along with a few on her bottom.
background: Attends nursery, where her parents mention a few other children have had "mouth ulcers and a fever" recently. Otherwise healthy and fully immunized for her age, no known allergies.

exam.title: General
exam.body: Ruby was miserable, reluctant to open her mouth, mildly dehydrated from reduced fluid intake, temperature 37.9°C.

exam.title: Mouth
exam.body: Several small, painful ulcers were seen scattered across the inside of her cheeks and on her tongue.

exam.title: Skin — hands and feet
exam.body: Small, oval, red-based blisters were seen on both palms and the soles of both feet, with a few similar lesions also present on her bottom — a distribution specific to this illness rather than the more widespread, trunk-predominant rash of a different childhood viral illness.

reports.title: Clinical Assessment Report
lines: Classic combination of mouth ulcers with blisters specifically on the palms, soles, and buttocks, distinguishing this from the more widespread rash of chickenpox and confirming the suspected diagnosis

investigations.title: Hydration
investigations.body: Given her reduced fluid intake, her hydration status was checked:

reports.title: Hydration Assessment
lines: Mild dehydration noted, though she remained able to take small sips of fluid, meaning intravenous fluids were not yet needed

treatment: Ruby was managed with simple pain relief to help with the discomfort from the mouth ulcers, encouragement to take cool, soft fluids and foods that wouldn't irritate her mouth further, and close monitoring of her hydration. Over the following few days, her fever settled, the mouth ulcers began to heal, and her appetite gradually returned.
discharge: She was kept home from nursery until she was feeling better and no longer had open blisters, with her parents given advice on hygiene measures to reduce the small risk of spreading it to other children in the household or at nursery.

title: Pulling at His Ear
personal: Ethan Walsh, 4, Male, 104 cm, 17 kg, preschooler. Seen in the pediatric assessment unit.
incident: For the past day Ethan has been pulling at his right ear repeatedly and has been unusually irritable, crying more than his mother would expect, particularly at night when lying down. He developed a fever overnight, and this morning complained clearly, for the first time being able to say it in words, that his ear hurts.
background: Had a runny nose and mild cold symptoms for about four days before the ear pain started. This is his second ear infection this year, previous episode resolved fully with a short course of antibiotics, no known allergies, up to date on immunizations.

exam.title: General
exam.body: Ethan was irritable but consolable, temperature 38.3°C, otherwise well and playful between bouts of ear pain.

exam.title: Ear examination
exam.body: The right eardrum appeared red, bulging, and inflamed, with reduced normal light reflection, consistent with fluid and pressure building up behind it, while the left ear looked entirely normal.

exam.title: Head and neck
exam.body: No swelling, redness, or tenderness over the bone behind either ear, and no facial weakness — findings that helped rule out a more serious spread of the infection.

reports.title: Ear Examination Report
lines: A bulging, inflamed eardrum on the right consistent with acute middle ear infection; left ear normal

investigations.title: Hearing
investigations.body: Given this was his second episode this year, a hearing check was arranged as a precaution:

reports.title: Hearing Assessment Report
lines: Mild, temporary reduction in hearing on the right side consistent with fluid behind the eardrum, expected to resolve once the infection clears

treatment: Ethan was started on a short course of oral antibiotics along with pain relief to help with the discomfort, particularly at night. Within two days his fever settled and the ear pain reduced substantially, and he returned to his usual cheerful self.
discharge: He completed his course of antibiotics at home, with a follow-up hearing check arranged in a few weeks to confirm his hearing had returned to normal, and a discussion with his parents about whether grommets might be worth considering if he continues to have frequent infections like this one.

title: A Bark in the Night
personal: Freddie Hastings, 2, Male, 88 cm, 13 kg, toddler. Seen in the pediatric emergency department.
incident: Freddie had a mild runny nose for the past two days, but tonight his parents were woken by a strange, harsh, barking cough coming from his room, along with a high-pitched noise every time he breathed in. He seemed frightened by his own cough, and his parents noticed his breathing looked like more effort than usual, though he was still talking and playing a little between coughing fits.
background: Previously well, no known asthma or breathing problems before, up to date on immunizations. An older sibling at home had a mild cold earlier in the week, no known allergies.

exam.title: General
exam.body: Freddie was alert, happily playing with a toy between coughing fits, mild fever of 38.1°C, no drooling, tolerating his own saliva without difficulty.

exam.title: Respiratory
exam.body: A distinctive harsh, barking cough was heard during the assessment, along with a high-pitched sound on breathing in that became more noticeable when he became upset or agitated, mild chest wall tugging seen with each breath when the noisy breathing was at its worst.

exam.title: ENT
exam.body: No drooling, no difficulty swallowing, voice sounded hoarse rather than muffled — findings that helped distinguish this from a different, more dangerous cause of noisy breathing in young children.

reports.title: Clinical Assessment Report
lines: Classic barking cough with a high-pitched breathing sound on inspiration, in a well-looking, non-drooling child, strongly supporting the suspected diagnosis over more concerning alternatives

investigations.title: Monitoring
investigations.body: His oxygen levels and breathing effort were monitored closely during the assessment:

reports.title: Monitoring Report
lines: Oxygen saturation remained normal throughout; breathing effort improved noticeably after treatment was given

treatment: Freddie was given a single dose of oral steroid medication to reduce the swelling in his airway, along with a short period of observation to make sure his breathing settled as expected. Within a couple of hours, the barking cough and noisy breathing had noticeably improved, and he was back to playing normally.
discharge: He was discharged home the same evening with advice on what to watch for if his breathing became more difficult again, reassurance that the cough might linger for a few more days even as he improved, and simple comfort measures to help him through it.

title: Too Tired to Finish the Bottle
personal: Baby Amelia Stokes, 4 months, Female, 62 cm, 6.2 kg, infant. Admitted to the pediatric ward.
incident: For the past three days Amelia has had a runny nose and mild cough, which her parents assumed was just an ordinary baby cold. Over the past day, though, her breathing has become noticeably faster and more labored, and she's been struggling to finish her bottles, needing to stop frequently to catch her breath, taking in far less milk than usual over the day.
background: Born full term, previously well, no history of breathing problems, an older sibling at nursery has had a cold this week, no known allergies, no smokers in the household.

exam.title: General
exam.body: Amelia was alert but working hard to breathe, respiratory rate 58, mild intercostal recession, oxygen saturation 93% on room air, feeding poorly during the assessment.

exam.title: Respiratory
exam.body: Widespread fine crackles were heard throughout both lungs, along with a mild wheeze, and her chest appeared slightly overinflated on inspection.

exam.title: General, further
exam.body: No fever, alert and responsive between coughing episodes, no signs of a heart murmur or other findings suggesting an underlying heart problem.

investigations.title: Laboratory
investigations.body: A swab from her nose was sent to identify the specific virus:

reports.title: Laboratory Report
lines: Respiratory viral swab: positive for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV)

investigations.title: Feeding
investigations.body: Her feeding and hydration were closely assessed given how much this was affecting her:

reports.title: Feeding Assessment Report
lines: Reduced but still adequate oral intake noted; close monitoring continued given the risk of this reducing further as the illness progresses

treatment: Amelia was supported with small, frequent feeds and, when her breathing effort made bottle feeding too tiring, some feeds were given through a small tube into her stomach to make sure she stayed properly hydrated and nourished, alongside supplemental oxygen and close monitoring of her breathing. Over the following three days, her breathing effort gradually eased, and she was able to return to taking full feeds by mouth.
discharge: She was discharged home once feeding well and breathing comfortably on room air, with advice for her parents on the usual course of this illness, when to seek help again if her breathing worsened, and simple measures to reduce the spread of the virus to her older sibling and others.

title: Hungry Again Right After
personal: Baby Jacob Turner, 5 weeks, Male, 56 cm, 4.5 kg, infant. Admitted to the pediatric surgical ward.
incident: Over the past week, Jacob's vomiting after feeds has become progressively more forceful, now shooting out with real force rather than the gentle spit-up his parents had gotten used to, sometimes reaching a foot or more away. Despite this, he seems hungry again almost immediately after vomiting and feeds eagerly, though his parents have noticed he seems to be gaining weight more slowly than expected at his last check-up, and today produced fewer wet nappies than usual.
background: Born full term, previously thriving on formula feeds, firstborn child, no family history that his parents are aware of, though his father mentioned, when asked, that he himself had "some kind of stomach operation" as a baby that nobody in the family remembers the details of.

exam.title: General
exam.body: Jacob was alert and hungry-looking despite the vomiting, mild weight loss compared with his growth chart trajectory, reduced skin turgor suggesting mild dehydration.

exam.title: Abdominal
exam.body: After being given a test feed, gentle palpation of the upper abdomen revealed a small, firm, olive-shaped lump, and a visible wave-like movement could be seen crossing his abdomen from left to right immediately after feeding — both findings specific to this particular condition.

exam.title: General, further
exam.body: No fever, urine output findings on questioning were reduced given his degree of dehydration, no signs of a rash or systemic illness.

investigations.title: Laboratory
investigations.body: Blood was sent to check his salt balance given the pattern of vomiting:

reports.title: Laboratory Report
lines: A specific pattern of electrolyte disturbance found — low chloride and potassium with an alkaline blood pH — a classic combination seen with this particular type of vomiting

investigations.title: Imaging
investigations.body: An ultrasound of his abdomen was arranged to look directly at the area felt on examination:

reports.title: Imaging Report
lines: The muscle at the outlet of the stomach was found to be thickened and elongated beyond the normal range for his age, confirming the cause of the obstruction

treatment: Jacob was first given fluids through a vein to correct his salt balance and dehydration before any procedure could safely go ahead, since operating before this is corrected can be dangerous. Once his levels had normalized, the surgical team performed a small operation. He was able to start small feeds again within a day of the procedure, tolerating increasing volumes without the forceful vomiting returning.
discharge: He went home a few days after the procedure, feeding well and gaining weight appropriately, with a routine follow-up appointment arranged to confirm his continued progress.

title: Slowing Down With Age
personal: Eleanor Pratt, 78, Female, 158 cm, 62 kg, retired librarian. Admitted to the intensive care unit.
incident: Her neighbor, who checks on her regularly through the winter, found her at home today unusually cold to the touch, extremely slow and sluggish in her responses, and slurring her words in a way that was completely out of character. Over recent weeks, the neighbor had noticed Eleanor seemed increasingly withdrawn, moving and speaking more slowly than before, and had put weight on despite eating less, all of which she'd assumed was just Eleanor "slowing down" with age.
background: Diagnosed with an underactive thyroid many years ago, prescribed a daily replacement tablet, though her neighbor later discovered a large stockpile of unused tablets at her home, suggesting she'd stopped taking them regularly some time ago. No other significant medical history that the neighbor was aware of, lives alone, limited family contact.

exam.title: General
exam.body: Eleanor was profoundly slow and sluggish in her responses, skin cool and dry to touch, temperature notably low at 34.2°C, heart rate 48 (slower than normal), blood pressure 92 over 58.

exam.title: Neurological
exam.body: Markedly slowed responses to questions, though ultimately answering appropriately once given extra time, no focal weakness, reflexes notably slow to relax after testing — a specific and telling finding in this condition.

exam.title: General, further
exam.body: Mild puffiness noted around her face and eyes, dry, coarse-feeling skin, and a hoarse quality to her voice.

reports.title: Laboratory Report
lines: TSH: markedly elevated
Free T4: very low
Sodium: low
Blood glucose: low-normal

investigations.title: Imaging
investigations.body: A CT scan of her head was performed given her profound slowness, to rule out a separate cause:

reports.title: Imaging Report
lines: No evidence of a stroke, no bleeding, no mass

treatment: Eleanor was started immediately on hormone treatment given directly into a vein, alongside gradual warming measures, careful fluid management, and close monitoring in intensive care given how unwell this particular condition can become. Over the following two to three days, her body temperature slowly returned to normal, her heart rate improved, and she became noticeably more alert and able to hold a proper conversation.
discharge: She was discharged once stable back onto her regular thyroid replacement tablets, with a proper system put in place, involving her neighbor and a local support service, to help make sure she takes her medication consistently going forward and has regular contact to check on her wellbeing.

title: Traveling From Knee to Ankle
personal: Sophia Alvarez, 9, Female, 132 cm, 30 kg, primary school student. Admitted to the pediatric ward.
incident: About three weeks after having a sore throat that wasn't seen by a doctor at the time, Sophia developed pain and swelling in her right knee, which seemed to settle after a couple of days only for her left ankle to become painful and swollen instead. Alongside this "traveling" joint pain, she's had a fever on and off, and her mother noticed yesterday that she seemed unusually breathless just walking up the stairs, along with some odd, jerky movements of her hands that she hadn't had before.
background: Previously healthy and active, the sore throat three weeks ago wasn't treated with antibiotics since her mother assumed it was "just a cold." No known heart problems before, up to date on immunizations, no family history of similar joint problems.

exam.title: General
exam.body: Sophia was looking generally unwell, temperature 38.4°C, heart rate elevated beyond what the fever alone would explain.

exam.title: Musculoskeletal
exam.body: Her left ankle was currently swollen, warm, and tender, while her right knee, though painful just days before, now looked and felt completely normal — a pattern of the pain "traveling" from joint to joint that doctors pay close attention to.

exam.title: Cardiovascular
exam.body: A new heart murmur was heard that hadn't been documented before, along with a heart rate faster than would be expected even accounting for her fever.

exam.title: Neurological/Skin
exam.body: Brief, jerky, uncontrollable movements were seen in both hands, and a faint, pink, ring-shaped rash was noted on her trunk that seemed to come and go as she was being examined.

investigations.title: Laboratory
investigations.body: Blood was sent to look for evidence of the preceding infection and current inflammation:

reports.title: Laboratory Report
lines: A blood test for recent streptococcal infection: positive
Inflammatory markers (ESR and CRP): both markedly elevated
Throat swab at this point: negative, as the original infection had already passed

investigations.title: Imaging
investigations.body: An echocardiogram was arranged given the new heart murmur:

reports.title: Imaging Report
lines: Mild leakiness identified in one of the heart valves, consistent with inflammation of the heart as part of this condition, with no evidence of an infection directly on the valve itself

treatment: Sophia was started on anti-inflammatory medication to settle the joint pain and inflammation, along with a course of antibiotics to fully clear any remaining infection, and close monitoring of her heart with the cardiology team involved given the murmur found on examination. Over the following two weeks, her joint pain resolved completely, the jerky hand movements settled, and her heart rate returned to normal.
discharge: She was discharged with a plan for long-term monthly antibiotic injections to prevent a recurrence, given how significantly repeat episodes can affect the heart over time, along with regular cardiology follow-up to monitor the mild valve changes found on her scan.

title: Missing Lectures for the First Time
personal: Ryan Kowalski, 19, Male, 178 cm, 74 kg, university student. Seen in the acute assessment unit.
incident: For the past week Ryan has had a severe sore throat, worse than any he can remember, making it painful to swallow even water, along with a fever and profound exhaustion that's kept him in bed for days, missing several lectures despite normally rarely being ill. This morning his roommate noticed his neck looked swollen on both sides, and Ryan mentioned feeling a dull ache in his upper left abdomen that he hadn't had before.
background: Lives in shared university accommodation, no significant past medical history, no known allergies, sexually active, mentions a new relationship starting a few weeks before his symptoms began, no recent antibiotics tried yet.

exam.title: General
exam.body: Ryan was visibly fatigued, temperature 38.9°C, otherwise stable vital signs.

exam.title: ENT
exam.body: His tonsils were markedly swollen and covered with a thick, white-grey coating on both sides, with swollen, tender lymph nodes felt on both sides of his neck as well as at the back of his neck — a distribution that helped distinguish this from a more localized bacterial throat infection.

exam.title: Abdominal
exam.body: Gentle palpation of his upper left abdomen revealed a mildly enlarged, though non-tender, spleen just below the ribs — a finding the doctor specifically checked for and noted carefully, since it changes advice about physical activity going forward.

investigations.title: Laboratory
investigations.body: Blood was sent, including a rapid test specific to this illness:

reports.title: Laboratory Report
lines: A rapid antibody test (heterophile antibody test): positive
Full blood count: showed an increased number of a particular type of white blood cell with an unusual appearance, typical of this illness
Throat swab for the bacterium causing strep throat: negative

reports.title: Laboratory Report
lines: Liver function tests: mildly elevated, a common and usually temporary finding with this particular infection

treatment: Ryan was managed with supportive care, including rest, fluids, and simple pain relief for his throat and fever, since this illness doesn't respond to antibiotics. He was specifically advised to avoid any contact sports or heavy lifting for several weeks given his enlarged spleen, which carries a small risk of rupture during this illness if injured. Over the following two to three weeks, his energy and throat symptoms gradually improved, though the fatigue took noticeably longer to fully resolve.
discharge: He was discharged with clear written advice about avoiding contact sports and heavy lifting for at least a month, along with reassurance that the profound tiredness some people feel with this illness can take several weeks to fully lift, and to return if he developed any severe abdominal pain suggesting his spleen had been affected.

title: Like Sandpaper
personal: Daisy Cooper, 6, Female, 118 cm, 22 kg, primary school student. Seen in the pediatric assessment unit.
incident: Two days ago Daisy developed a sore throat and fever, and yesterday her mother noticed a fine, rough, red rash appearing on her chest that felt "like sandpaper" when she ran her hand over it. The rash has since spread to her arms and legs, and today her mother noticed her tongue looked unusually red and bumpy, almost like a strawberry.
background: Previously healthy, up to date on immunizations, several classmates at school have had sore throats recently, no known allergies, no previous episodes of a similar rash.

exam.title: General
exam.body: Daisy was unwell but alert, temperature 38.6°C, heart rate mildly elevated in keeping with the fever.

exam.title: Skin
exam.body: A fine, red, rough-textured rash with a sandpaper-like quality was felt across her chest, arms, and legs, sparing the area around her mouth, which appeared notably pale in contrast to her flushed cheeks.

exam.title: ENT/Mouth
exam.body: Her tonsils were red and swollen with white patches, and her tongue had a strikingly red, bumpy, strawberry-like appearance; tender, swollen lymph nodes were felt in her neck.

investigations.title: Laboratory
investigations.body: A swab was taken from the back of her throat:

reports.title: Laboratory Report
lines: Rapid strep test: positive for the bacterium responsible for strep throat and this associated rash

investigations.title: Laboratory
investigations.body: Routine blood tests were sent to check her general inflammatory response:

reports.title: Laboratory Report
lines: White cell count: raised
CRP: elevated, in keeping with a bacterial infection

treatment: Daisy was started on a course of antibiotics to treat the underlying infection, along with fever medication for her comfort. Within a day of starting the antibiotics, her fever began to settle, and over the following week the rash gradually faded, with some peeling of the skin on her hands as it resolved, which the family was told to expect.
discharge: She completed her full course of antibiotics at home and was kept away from school until 24 hours after starting treatment and no longer feeling unwell, as advised, to reduce the risk of passing the infection on to her classmates.

title: Craving Ice
personal: Rachel Owusu, 35, Female, 165 cm, 63 kg, nurse. Seen in outpatient assessment.
incident: Over the past couple of months, Rachel has noticed herself becoming increasingly tired despite getting what should be adequate sleep, finding herself breathless climbing the stairs at the hospital where she works, something that's never bothered her before. She's also noticed an unusual craving to chew on ice cubes, which she finds a little embarrassing to mention, along with her heavier-than-usual periods over the past several months.
background: Has had consistently heavy periods for the past year that she'd been managing herself rather than seeking help for, follows a diet with limited red meat intake by personal preference, no known gastrointestinal problems, no family history of any blood disorders, not currently pregnant.

exam.title: General
exam.body: Rachel had a pale complexion, particularly in the lining of her lower eyelids and the creases of her palms, otherwise stable vital signs with a mildly elevated heart rate.

exam.title: Cardiovascular
exam.body: A soft flow murmur was heard — a common and usually harmless finding when someone's blood carries less oxygen-delivering capacity than normal, rather than a sign of a structural heart problem.

exam.title: General, further
exam.body: Mildly brittle-looking nails were noted, with a subtle spoon-shaped indentation on a couple of her fingernails — a specific sign doctors associate with a significant, longstanding version of this condition.

investigations.title: Laboratory
investigations.body: Blood was sent for a full count and specific iron studies:

reports.title: Laboratory Report
lines: Hemoglobin: low
Red blood cells: notably smaller than normal on the blood film
Ferritin (the body's iron store): markedly low
Vitamin B12 and folate levels: both normal, arguing against the alternative type of anemia being considered

investigations.title: Assessment
investigations.body: Given her heavy periods, and to check for any other source of blood loss given her age, further assessment was arranged:

reports.title: Assessment Report
lines: Gynecological review arranged to investigate the cause of her heavy periods directly; no other symptoms suggesting blood loss from elsewhere were identified on questioning

treatment: Rachel was started on replacement tablets, with advice on how to take them to maximize absorption and minimize stomach upset, while her heavy periods were addressed in parallel with the gynecology team to treat the underlying cause of her ongoing blood loss. Over the following two months, her energy levels and breathlessness gradually improved as her blood results recovered.
discharge: She continued her iron supplements for several months to fully replenish her stores, with a repeat blood count arranged to confirm full recovery, alongside ongoing management of her heavy periods to prevent this from recurring.
dd1: Vitamin B12 deficiency anemia or Folate deficiency anemia

title: Pulled Over Shaking
personal: Dennis Hargrove, 55, Male, 178 cm, 84 kg, taxi driver, known type 2 diabetes on insulin. Admitted to the acute medical unit.
incident: While driving a fare this afternoon, Dennis suddenly felt shaky, sweaty, and lightheaded, with his heart pounding and his vision blurring slightly, forcing him to pull over. His passenger, noticing him becoming confused and slurring his words, called for help. By the time paramedics arrived, he seemed disoriented and was struggling to answer simple questions correctly.
background: Type 2 diabetes for 15 years, started on insulin injections about a year ago. He admits he skipped lunch today because of a busy shift but still took his usual insulin dose this morning. No known kidney or liver problems, no alcohol that day.

exam.title: General
exam.body: Dennis was pale, sweating profusely, and trembling, confused but rousable. Heart rate 112, blood pressure 138 over 84.

exam.title: Neurological
exam.body: Disoriented to time, slow and slurred speech, no facial droop, no limb weakness, pupils equal and reactive.

exam.title: General, further
exam.body: No smell of alcohol on his breath, no evidence of a seizure such as tongue biting or incontinence.

investigations.title: Laboratory
investigations.body: A fingerprick blood sugar test was checked immediately at the roadside and again on arrival:

reports.title: Laboratory Report
lines: Capillary blood glucose: markedly low, well below the normal range

investigations.title: Laboratory
investigations.body: Given how quickly his confusion resolved with treatment, further testing was kept minimal, but routine bloods were sent to check for an underlying cause:

reports.title: Laboratory Report
lines: Kidney function: normal
No evidence of infection or other illness that might have contributed to the low blood sugar

treatment: Dennis was given a fast-acting treatment by mouth, followed by a snack once he was able to swallow safely, along with close monitoring over the following hours. Within fifteen minutes of the first treatment, his confusion cleared completely and he was back to his usual self, embarrassed but otherwise well.
discharge: He was discharged with a review of his insulin dosing and meal timing with a diabetes nurse, advice on always carrying a fast-acting sugar source and checking his blood sugar before driving, and a reminder of the importance of never skipping meals when taking insulin.
dd1: Diabetic ketoacidosis or Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state

title: A Couple of Hours After Eating
personal: Cynthia Palmer, 45, Female, 160 cm, 66 kg, accountant. Seen in outpatient gastroenterology clinic.
incident: For the past six weeks, Cynthia has had a recurring, gnawing pain in her upper abdomen that tends to come on a couple of hours after eating and sometimes wakes her at night, which she's found is eased somewhat by eating a small snack or taking antacids. She hasn't vomited blood or noticed black stools, and she's not lost any weight, but the discomfort has become frequent enough that she decided to get it checked out.
background: Takes ibuprofen occasionally for tension headaches, drinks coffee daily, moderate social alcohol use, no known ulcers before, no family history of stomach cancer, no smoking.

exam.title: General
exam.body: Cynthia was well-looking, comfortable, with normal vital signs.

exam.title: Abdominal
exam.body: Mild tenderness in the upper-middle abdomen on deep palpation, no mass, no guarding, no signs suggesting anything more serious such as weight loss or difficulty swallowing.

investigations.title: Laboratory
investigations.body: Given her symptoms had been present for several weeks, a breath test was arranged to check for a specific stomach bacterium:

reports.title: Laboratory Report
lines: Urea breath test: positive for Helicobacter pylori infection

investigations.title: Endoscopy
investigations.body: Given the duration of her symptoms, an endoscopy was arranged to directly visualize the lining of her stomach:

reports.title: Endoscopy Report
lines: A small ulcer identified in the lining of the stomach, with no signs of bleeding or any suspicious features
Biopsies taken confirmed no evidence of cancer

treatment: Cynthia was started on a course of medication alongside a combination of antibiotics, and advised to stop taking ibuprofen and switch to a different pain reliever for her headaches. Over the following weeks, her abdominal discomfort gradually resolved.
discharge: She completed her course of treatment, with a follow-up breath test arranged in a couple of months to confirm the bacterium had been fully cleared, and advice on avoiding anti-inflammatory painkillers going forward given her history.

title: Dazed After the Tackle
personal: Jordan Ellis, 17, Male, 178 cm, 72 kg, high school student and rugby player. Seen in the emergency department.
incident: During a match this afternoon, Jordan took a hard hit to the side of his head during a tackle, and though he didn't lose consciousness, he seemed dazed and confused for a minute or two afterward, unable to remember the details of the play that had just happened. He came off the field complaining of a headache and feeling a bit sick, and has vomited once since arriving at the hospital.
background: No previous head injuries or concussions, no significant past medical history, not on any blood thinners, no known bleeding disorders, played a full match last week without incident.

exam.title: General
exam.body: Jordan was alert, mildly slow to answer some questions, oriented to person, place, and time on repeat testing, with normal vital signs.

exam.title: Neurological
exam.body: No focal weakness, normal pupil reactions on both sides, no neck tenderness. He was able to recall the events shortly before the injury with some difficulty, though not the injury itself.

exam.title: Head/Skin
exam.body: A small area of swelling was felt over the side of his head where he was struck, no visible skull deformity, no bruising behind his ears or around his eyes that might suggest a skull base fracture.

investigations.title: Clinical
investigations.body: His case was carefully assessed against the specific criteria doctors use to decide who needs a scan after a head injury:

reports.title: Clinical Assessment Report
lines: No high-risk features identified requiring an urgent CT scan (no loss of consciousness beyond a brief moment, no worsening headache, no seizure, no focal neurological findings, no signs of a skull fracture), supporting a period of observation over immediate imaging

investigations.title: Observation
investigations.body: He was kept for a period of observation with regular neurological checks:

reports.title: Observation Report
lines: No deterioration in his alertness or neurological findings over several hours of monitoring

treatment: Jordan was managed with rest, simple pain relief for his headache, and clear guidance on gradually returning to normal activities, with strict instructions to avoid any contact sports until fully cleared. His headache and nausea settled over the following day with rest.
discharge: He was discharged with written head injury advice for his parents, including signs that should prompt an urgent return, and a structured, step-by-step plan for returning to school and eventually sport only once he'd been fully symptom-free for a period of time, in line with standard concussion recovery guidance.

title: Keys in the Refrigerator
